*

Monotonicity of the Relative Entropy and the Two-sided Bogoliubov Inequality in von Neumann Algebras

Benedikt M. Reible Electronic mail: benedikt.reible@fu-berlin.de

Institut für Theoretische Physik, Universität Leipzig

June, 2024

## Abstract

This text studies, on the one hand, certain monotonicity properties of the Araki-Uhlmann relative entropy and, on the other hand, unbounded perturbation theory of KMS-states which facilitates a proof of the two-sided Bogoliubov inequality in general von Neumann algebras. After introducing the necessary background from the theory of operator algebras and Tomita-Takesaki modular theory, the relative entropy functional is defined and its basic properties are studied. In particular, a full and detailed proof of Uhlmann's important monotonicity theorem for the relative entropy is provided. This theorem will then be used to derive a number of monotonicity inequalities for the relative entropy of normal functionals induced by vectors of the form $V \Omega, V \Phi \in \MH$, where $V \in \BO(\MH)$ is a suitable transformation. After that, an introduction to perturbation theory in von Neumann algebras is given, with an emphasis on unbounded perturbations of KMS-states following the framework of Derezi\'nski-Jak i\'c-Pillet. This mathematical apparatus will then be used to extend the two-sided Bogoliubov inequality for the relative free energy, which was very recently proved for quantum-mechanical systems, to arbitrary von Neumann algebras.

# Introduction

In recent years, a substantial interest in information-theoretic aspects of quantum field theory has developed. An indispensible tool in corresponding studies is the relative entropy functional which was already defined in 1977 in its most general form for arbitrary von Neumann algebras. Lately, it has experienced a renaissance in mathematical physics, especially in algebraic quantum field theory, with many new applications being discovered and investigated. To motivate the specific problems studied in the present text, the use of the relative entropy in mathematical physics is reviewed briefly in [ref:sec:introduction_history]. Following this, [ref:sec:introduction_outline] provides a concise outline of the text.

## The Relative Entropy in Mathematical Physics

#sec:introduction_history

[The Kullback-Leibler divergence]#para:inroduction_KL
The notion of relative entropy was first introduced in mathematical statistics by and in 1951 [cite:KullbackLeibler51]. In modern terminology, it can be defined as follows: let $(\Omega, \Sigma)$ be a measurable space and $P, Q$ be two probability measures on $\Sigma$ such that $P$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $Q$. In this case, the Radon-Nikodým derivative $\od{P}{Q}$ exists [cite:Cohn13], and the or between $P$ and $Q$ is defined to be [cite:Jaksic19]

[equation:eq:introduction_KL]
$$
D(P, Q) \ce \int_\Omega \log\left(\od{P}{Q}\right) \diff P = \int_\Omega \od{P}{Q} \, \log\left(\od{P}{Q}\right) \diff Q \ .
$$

If $P$ is not absolutely continuous with respect to $Q$, one can extend the above definition by setting $D(P, Q) \ce + \infty$. [ref:eq:introduction_KL] has a number of interesting properties, for example [cite:Jaksic19]:

[num]

- #enu:introduction_KLposdef $D(P, Q) \ge 0$ and $D(P, Q) = 0$ if and only if $P = Q$;

- #enu:introduction_KLmonotonicity $D\bigl(\alpha(P), \alpha(Q)\bigr) \le D(P, Q)$ for every stochastic mapping $\alpha$;

- #enu:introduction_KLconvex $(P, Q) \longmto D(P, Q)$ is jointly convex.

Based on [ref:enu:introduction_KLposdef], the relative entropy $D(P, Q)$ can be interpreted as a measure for the distinguishability of the probability distributions $P$ and $Q$ [cite:OP04]. In fact, it can be shown that if one draws $N$ samples according to $Q$, then the probability that they will look as if they were drawn from $P$ is proportional to $\exp(- N D(P, Q))$ for large $N$ [cite:Vedral02]. In light of this interpretation, [ref:enu:introduction_KLmonotonicity] implies that the probability distributions $P$ and $Q$ can only become less distinguishable under stochastic evolution [cite:Vedral02], and property [ref:enu:introduction_KLconvex] asserts that mixing probability distributions decreases distinguishability [cite:Vedral02].

The notion of distinguishability is of fundamental importance for information theory because the degree to which one can distinguish between different physical states of a system determines the amount of information that can be encoded and manipulated [cite:Vedral02]. This is the main reason why generalizations of the relative entropy [ref:eq:introduction_KL] to non-commutative probability spaces have become so important in quantum information theory and quantum field theory, as will be outlined in the following.

[The Umegaki relative entropy]#para:introduction_Umegaki
Let $\MH$ be a Hilbert space. The Kullback-Leibler divergence [ref:eq:introduction_KL] was extended to the von Neumann algebra $\MFM = \BO(\MH)$ by in 1962 [cite:Umegaki62]: if $\omega$ and $\varphi$ are two normal states on $\MFM$ represented by density matrices $\rho_\omega, \rho_\varphi \in \DM(\MH)$ such that $\ker(\rho_\omega)^\perp \subset \ker(\rho_\varphi)^\perp$, then the or of $\omega$ with respect to $\varphi$ is defined to be [cite:OP04]

[equation:eq:introduction_Umegaki]
$$
S(\rho_\omega, \rho_\varphi) \ce \tr\bigl(\rho_\omega (\log \rho_\omega - \log \rho_\varphi)\bigr) \ .
$$

One can show that if $\rho_\omega$ and $\rho_\varphi$ commute with each other, then [ref:eq:introduction_Umegaki] reduces to [ref:eq:introduction_KL] [cite:OP04]. Furthermore, analoga of the properties [ref:enu:introduction_KLposdef] -- [ref:enu:introduction_KLconvex] from [ref:para:inroduction_KL] can be proved for the Umegaki entropy as well [cite:OP04]. Therefore, one can interpret the quantity $S(\omega, \varphi)$ as a measure for the distinguishability of $\omega$ and $\varphi$ [cite:Vedral02].

The relative entropy [ref:eq:introduction_Umegaki] was introduced to mathematical physics by in 1973 -- 1975 [cite:Lindblad73, Lindblad74, Lindblad75]. He used this quantity to analyze the quantum-mechanical measurement process, and he showed that $S$ is non-increasing under completely positive maps; see [cite:MHReeb17, Petz03] for recent discussions and refinements of this monotonicity property. Since then, the quantum relative entropy has become an indispensible tool in two areas of mathematical physics: statistical mechanics [cite:Wehrl78] and quantum information theory [cite:Schumacher00, Vedral02]. In the former, Lindblad's monotonicity result can be seen as a for open quantum systems [cite:GustafsonSigal20], and the analogue of [ref:para:inroduction_KL] [ref:enu:introduction_KLposdef] can be used to prove that the canonical Gibbs state is the unique minimizer of the free energy [cite:OP04]. Recently, there have also been studies which suggest reformulations of the second and third law of thermodynamics using the relative entropy [cite:DowlingFloerchingerHaas20, FloerchingerHaas20, Sagawa23]. In quantum information theory, the Umegaki relative entropy plays a role analogous to that of the Kullback-Leibler divergence in classical statistics [cite:Vedral02]. Among other reasons, this is due to the fact that the relative entropy can be used to quantify the amount of entanglement present in a single quantum state [cite:Schumacher00], [cite:Vedral02].

Lately, also an interest in entanglement measures for relativistic quantum field theory has developed, see the overviews [cite:HollandsSanders18, Witten18] and other references given below in [ref:para:introduction_ArakiUhlmann]. Since the Umegaki relative entropy is not available for general quantum field theories [cite:LongoXu18], a more general definition of a relative entropy functional is needed.

[The Araki-Uhlmann relative entropy]#para:introduction_ArakiUhlmann
A generalization of the Umegaki relative entropy to arbitrary von Neumann algebras was discovered by in 1977, who had previously already made substantial contributions to the mathematical theory of von Neumann algebras ( , [cite:Araki74a, ArakiWoods68]) and algebraic quantum field theory ( , [cite:Araki63, Araki64b, Araki64a]). He developed an extension of Tomita-Takesaki modular theory and used it to define a notion of relative entropy $\MS_\MFM(\omega, \varphi)$ between normal functionals $\omega, \varphi$ on an arbitrary von Neumann algebra $\MFM$ [cite:Araki76, Araki77]. To some extend, he was motivated by questions of statistical mechanics regarding certain properties of KMS-states, where he had already applied methods from modular theory and perturbation theory in operator algebras [cite:Araki74b, Araki75].

Simultaneously and independently, also introduced a notion of relative entropy between positive linear functionals on $\ast$-algebras using an abstract quadratic interpolation theory [cite:Uhlmann77]. Later, it was shown by that 's and 's definition actually coincide on von Neumann algebras [cite:Petz86a], [cite:OP04], whence this functional, which is the protagonist of this text, is termed the Araki-Uhlmann relative entropy; it will be formally introduced in [ref:def:relativeEntropy_stdRelativeEntropy,def:relativeEntropy_spaRelativeEntropy]. In [cite:Uhlmann77], also proved a very general monotonicity theorem for the relative entropy which generalizes Lindblad's result mentioned in [ref:para:introduction_Umegaki]. Namely, he showed that for a unital normal Schwarz mapping $\alpha : \MFM_1 \longto \MFM_2$, the following inequality holds true [cite:OP04]

[equation:eq:introduction_UhlmannMonotonicity]
$$
\MS_{\MFM_1}(\omega \circ \alpha, \varphi \circ \alpha) \le \MS_{\MFM_2}(\omega, \varphi) \ .
$$

This property of the relative entropy is highly important for many reasons, , the fact that analoga of [ref:enu:introduction_KLposdef] and [ref:enu:introduction_KLconvex] from [ref:para:inroduction_KL] can be proved with the help of [ref:eq:introduction_UhlmannMonotonicity]; [ref:sec:relativeEntropy_monotonicity] of this text is devoted to this topic. Further properties of the Araki-Uhlmann relative entropy were studied in the 80s and 90s by [cite:Donald86, Donald87b], [cite:Kosaki86], and [cite:Petz86a, Petz86b, Petz88, Petz91, Petz92, Petz94], to name just a selected few.

After the introduction of the relative entropy on general von Neumann algebras, it was primarily applied in statistical mechanics to study KMS-states [cite:ArakiSewell77, BR2]. The interest of quantum field theorists in the relative entropy started only a couple of years ago. To the best knowledge of the author, this can be traced back to a paper of from 2008 [cite:Casini08] who used the Umegaki relative entropy [ref:eq:introduction_Umegaki] to give a proof of the so-called Bekenstein bound which provides an upper limit for the entropy of a system in terms of its energy and size. Ten years later, and [cite:LongoXu18] pointed out that 's argument breaks down for general quantum field theories, and they gave a more rigorous proof of the Bekenstein bound using the Araki-Uhlmann relative entropy. Since then, this quantity has been applied to various problems in (algebraic) quantum field theory (in curved spacetimes). To begin with, et al. [cite:CGP19] and [cite:Longo19] independently computed, in the setting of a free scalar field, the relative entropy between the vacuum state and a coherent excitation thereof; generalizations of these computations were considered afterwards by various authors [cite:Hollands20, BCV22, BCM23, Galanda23]. Furthermore, a connection between the relative entropy and quantum energy inequalities was discovered by and [cite:CeyhanFaulkner2020] (see also [cite:CLRR22, MTW22, Wall17]), and more general investigations of relativistic quantum information theory were conducted by , , , and others [cite:CLR20, FaulknerHollands2022, FHSW2022, FMP23, Hiai18a, Hiai19, Hiai21a, Hollands21, Hollands23, HollandsIshibashi19, HollandsSanders18, Longo20].

## Outline of the Text

#sec:introduction_outline

As illustrated above, the study of the relative entropy in von Neumann algebras is a highly active field of research. It is the goal of this text to contribute to this field by providing a detailed introduction to its mathematical foundations, and by discussing certain properties of the relative entropy related to monotonicity and perturbation theory of KMS-states. To this end, [ref:ch:operatorAlgebras] gives an overview of the theory of $C^\ast$-algebras and von Neumann algebras, and [ref:ch:vonNeumann] contains a fairly detailed discussion of Tomita-Takesaki modular theory.

The Araki-Uhlmann relative entropy is introduced in [ref:ch:relativeEntropy], first for von Neumann algebras in standard form, and second for arbitrary representations. The main part of this chapter is devoted to the monotonicity theorem of . Fully detailed proofs of this result and of all the auxiliary lemmata required to establish it are presented; in this form, this is not readily available in the literature. [ref:sec:relativeEntropy_vectorMonotonicity] contains some original results regarding the following question: given von Neumann algebras $\MFM_1, \MFM_2 \subset \BO(\MH)$ and vectors $\Omega, \Phi \in \MH$, for which Hilbert-space transformations $V \in \BO(\MH)$ can one prove monotonicity inequalities of the form $\MS_{\MFM_1}(V \Omega, V \Phi) \le \MS_{\MFM_2}(\Omega, V)$? Results along these lines will be obtained by applying Uhlmann's general theorem to specific situations (see [ref:pro:relativeEntropy_vectorMonotonicityIsometry,eq:relativeEntropy_vectorMonotonicityIsometry2,pro:relativeEntropy_vectorMonotonicityPartialIsometry,pro:relativeEntropy_vectorMonotonicityUnitary,pro:vectorMonotonicity_contraction]).

In [ref:ch:perturbationTheory], perturbation theory in operator algebras is discussed. Primarily, the chapter deals with unbounded perturbations of KMS-states by reviewing relatively recent results of J. Derezi\'nski, V. Jak i\'c, and [cite:DJP03], and extending them slightly in [ref:subsec:perturbationTheory_unboundedPerturbationKMS] (see [ref:lem:perturbationTheory_unboundedConvergenceLiouvillian] [ref:enu:perturbationTheory_unbdConvergenceSum], [ref:thm:perturbationTheory_unboundedPerturbation] [ref:enu:perturbationTheory_unboundedRelModOp2], and [ref:pro:perturbationTheory_relEntUnboundedPerturbedState]). The final [ref:sec:perturbationTheory_twoSidedBogoliubov] is concerned with the so-called two-sided Bogoliubov inequality. This inequality was first discussed in the setting of classical statistical mechanics as a tool to estimate finite-size effects in molecular simulations [cite:DS17]. It was extended to quantum statistical mechanics by the author of this text in his bachelor's thesis; the findings were published in [cite:Reible22] (they will be reviewed very briefly in [ref:subsec:perturbationTheory_twoSidedBogoliubovQM]), and concrete applications of this inequality to different problems were subsequently presented in [cite:Reible23, DS24]. In this work, using the extended framework of unbounded perturbation theory of KMS-states, the results of [cite:Reible22] are generalized to the setting of arbitrary von Neumann algebras. First, a version of the two-sided Bogoliubov inequality is obtained ([ref:pro:perturbationTheory_BogoliubovVN]) which reduces to the known inequality of [cite:Reible22] on the von Neumann algebra $\BO(\MH)$. Second, the variational bounds of [cite:Reible22] are extended to certain classes of unbounded perturbations in [ref:subsec:perturbationTheory_variationalBoundsVN] (see [ref:pro:perturbationTheory_unboundedGibbsVP,pro:perturabtionTheory_unboundedDVVP] as well as [ref:cor:perturbationTheory_unboundedVariationalBounds]).

The main part of text will be concluded with [ref:ch:conclusion] which summarizes the results and provides a brief outlook. Finally, [ref:app:topologicalVectorSpaces,app:operators,app:forms] contain some selected definitions and results from the fields of topological vector spaces, (un)bounded linear operators, and quadratic forms on Hilbert spaces which are needed throughout the text.

# Aspects of the Theory of Operator Algebras

#ch:operatorAlgebras

To commence the study of the Araki-Uhlmann relative entropy, this chapter presents some basic definitions and results from the mathematically rich theory of operator algebras. First, [ref:sec:operatorAlgebras_CStar] introduces $C^\ast$-algebras and their positive elements. Following that, [ref:sec:operatorAlgebras_positiveMaps] studies properties of positive mappings between $C^\ast$-algebras. In [ref:sec:operatorAlgebras_vonNeumann], the important subclass of von Neumann algebras and some of their basic properties are discussed. Finally, [ref:sec:operatorAlgebras_representationsStates] presents the important GNS-construction. Due to the vastness of the theory, the limited amount of space available, and the wide range of literature on the topic, only a few selected proofs will be given.

The main source for this chapter is [cite:BR1]. In addition, the following references were consulted: [cite:BärFredenhagen09], [cite:BlanchardBrüning15], [cite:BonsallDuncan73], [cite:Conway85], [cite:Sakai98], [cite:Schmüdgen20], [cite:StratilaZsido19], [cite:Takesaki79], and [cite:Werner18].

## $C^\ast$-Algebras

C*-Algebras#sec:operatorAlgebras_CStar

### Definitions and Examples

The properties characterizing $C^\ast$-algebras are, on the one hand, an abstraction of properties displayed by the space $(\BO(\MH), \ndot_\mop)$ of bounded linear operators on a Hilbert space $\MH$. On the other hand, the class of $C^\ast$-algebras forms a subclass of the more general Banach algebras, characterized by additional requirements on the algebra norm. Here, the definition of a $C^\ast$-algebra shall be presented directly without a deductive tour through the theory of Banach algebras; for the latter, see [cite:BonsallDuncan73, KadisonRingrose97, Takesaki79]. First, however, some purely algebraic concepts are recalled.

[$\ast$-algebras]#para:operatorAlgebras_astAlgebras
([cite:BonsallDuncan73], [cite:Schmüdgen20])
A is a $\K$-algebra together with an algebra involution $\MFA \longto \MFA$, $A \longmto A^\ast$, that is, a mapping satisfying for all $A, B \in \MFA$ and $\lambda, \mu \in \K$:

$$
(A^\ast)^\ast = A \com (\lambda \cdot A + \mu \cdot B)^\ast = \ol{\lambda} \cdot A^\ast + \ol{\mu} \cdot B^\ast \ , \tand (AB)^\ast = B^\ast A^\ast \ .
$$

A subset $\MFJ \subset \MFA$ is called self-adjoint iff $A^\ast \in \MFJ$ for every $A \in \MFJ$, and a self-adjoint subalgebra (ideal) of $\MFA$ is called a $\ast$-subalgebra ($\ast$-ideal). An element $A \in \MFA$ is called iff $A^\ast = A$, and the set of all self-adjoint elements is denoted by $\SE{\MFA}$. This set is a real linear subspace of $\MFA$ such that $\MFA = \SE{\MFA} \oplus_\R \ii \, \SE{\MFA}$ [cite:BonsallDuncan73]. A linear mapping $f : \MFA \longto \MFB$ between two $\ast$-algebras is called a iff $f(AB) = f(A) f(B)$ and $f(A^\ast) = f(A)^\ast$ for all $A, B \in \MFA$. Finally, an element $A \in \MFA$ of a unital $\ast$-algebra $(\MFA, \idm)$ is called iff there exists an element $\inv{A} \in \MFA$ such that $A \inv{A} = \inv{A} A = \idm$. The set of all invertible elements of $\MFA$ is denoted by $\GL(\MFA)$.

## Definition: $C^\ast$-algebra [label:def:operatorAlgebras_CStar]

Let $\MFA$ be a $\ast$-algebra. If there exists a norm $\ndot : \MFA \longto [0, + \infty)$ such that (1) $\MFA$ is $\ndot$-complete, (2) $\ndot$ is sub-multiplicative, that is,

$$
\forall A, B \in \MFA \ : \ \norm{AB} \le \norm{A} \, \norm{B} \ ,
$$

and (3) $\ndot$ satisfies the the so-called $C^\ast$-property

$$
\forall A \in \MFA \ : \ \norm{A^\ast A} = \norm{A}^2 \ ,
$$

then $(\MFA, \ndot)$ is called an ,
The terminology will be apparent after concrete $C^\ast$-algebras are introduced in [ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaConcreteCstar]. The name was coined by in 1947 [cite:Segal47].
and $\ndot$ is called a $C^\ast$-algebra norm. If there is no risk of confusion, such an algebra will be called $C^\ast$-algebra and denoted by $\MFA$ for short. The algebra norm $\ndot$ defines a metric topology on $\MFA$ which is referred to as the or $\MFT_norm$. Finally, a of $\MFA$ is defined to be a uniformly closed $\ast$-subalgebra $\MFB \subset \MFA$.

#exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar

[env]

- The complex numbers $\C$ form a commutative $C^\ast$-algebra with involution given by complex conjugation $z = a + \ii b \longmto \ol{z} \ce a - \ii b$ and norm given by the absolute value.

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaCCStar Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space and $C^0(X) \ce C^0(X; \C)$ be the space of continuous functions $f : X \longto \C$. With multiplication defined pointwise, $(fg)(x) \ce f(x) g(x)$ for $f, g \in C^0(X)$ and $x \in X$, involution given by $f^\ast(x) \ce \ol{f(x)}$, and norm defined to be

$$
\norm{f}_\infty \ce \sup_{x \in X} \abs{f(x)} \ ,
$$

this space becomes a commutative $C^\ast$-algebra [cite:BR1]. It is unital with unit given by the constant function $\1_X : X \longto \K$, $x \longmto 1$.

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaLInfCStar Similarly to the previous example, for a measure space $(\Omega, \Sigma, \mu)$ it holds that the essentially bounded functions $L^\infty(\Omega, \mu)$ with pointwise multiplication, the involution from [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaCCStar], and the essential supremum norm $\ndot_{L^\infty}$ form a unital commutative $C^\ast$-algebra.

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaMatCStar Let $n \in \N$. The space $\Mat(n; \K)$ consisting of $(n \times n)$-matrices with entries in $\K$ is a unital $\K$-algebra with multiplication given by the matrix product. If $\K = \R$, one can define an involution in terms of the transposition $A \longmto \tran{A}$, and if $\K = \C$, an involution is given by $A \longmto \tran{(\ol{A})}$. There exist various sub-multiplicative, complete norms on $\Mat(n; \K)$, , the Frobenius norm [cite:Werner22], but only the operator norm satisfies the $C^\ast$-property [cite:BR1].

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaBOCStar Let $(\MH, \bdot)$ be a Hilbert space. The space $\BO(\MH)$ of bounded linear operators $T : \MH \longto \MH$ is a unital $\ast$-algebra with multiplication $(T, S) \longmto T \circ S \equiv TS$ and involution given by the operation $T \longmto T^\ast$ of taking adjoints. Furthermore, the [cite:Werner18]

$$
\norm{T}_\mop \ce \norm{T}_{\BO(\MH)} \ce \sup_{\xi \in \MH \setminus \{0\}} \frac{\norm{T \xi}}{\norm{\xi}} = \sup_{\norm{\xi} \le 1} \norm{T \xi} = \sup_{\norm{\xi} = 1} \norm{T \xi}
$$

is sub-multiplicative because for $T, S \in \BO(\MH)$ and $\xi \in \MH$, the inequality

$$
\norm{T (S \xi)} \le \norm{T}_\mop \norm{S \xi} \le \norm{T}_\mop \norm{S}_\mop \norm{\xi} \ ,
$$

which follows from boundedness of $T$ and $S$, implies $\norm{T S}_\mop \le \norm{T}_\mop \norm{S}_\mop$ [cite:Werner18]. It holds that $(\BO(\MH), \ndot_\mop)$ is complete [cite:Werner18], and the involution satisfies $\norm{T^\ast}_\mop = \norm{T}_\mop$ [cite:Werner18]. Finally, for all $T \in \BO(\MH)$ and $\xi \in \MH$, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality implies

$$
\norm{T \xi}^2 = \braket{T \xi, T \xi} = \braket{\xi, T^\ast T \xi} \le \norm{\xi} \, \norm{T^\ast T \xi} \ .
$$

With this inequality and [ref:eq:operatorAlgebras_algebraNorm], it follows that

$$
\norm{T}_\mop^2 &= \sup_{\norm{\xi} \le 1} \norm{T \xi}^2 \le \sup_{\norm{\xi} \le 1} \norm{\xi} \, \norm{T^\ast T \xi} \le \norm{T^\ast T}_\mop \le \norm{T^\ast}_\mop \norm{T}_\mop = \norm{T}_\mop^2 \ .
$$

This chain of inequalities shows that there is actually equality, , $\norm{T^\ast T}_\mop = \norm{T}_\mop^2$ for all $T \in \BO(\MH)$, hence $(\BO(\MH), \ndot_\mop)$ is a unital $C^\ast$-algebra [cite:Werner18].

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaKOCStar Let $\KO(\MH) \subset \BO(\MH)$ be the space of compact operators on $\MH$. It holds that $\KO(\MH)$ is a $\ndot_\mop$-closed subalgebra of $\BO(\MH)$ [cite:Werner18] which is not unital if $\dim(\MH) = + \infty$ [cite:Werner18]. Furthermore, $T \in \KO(\MH)$ if and only if $T^\ast \in \KO(\MH)$ [cite:Werner18], hence $\KO(\MH)$ is a normed $\ast$-ideal of $\BO(\MH)$, and thus, in particular, a $C^\ast$-algebra as well.

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaNOHSCStar The space $\NO(\MH)$ of trace-class operators and the space $\HS(\MH)$ of Hilbert-Schmidt operators ([ref:def:operators_NOHS]) are $\ast$-ideals in $\BO(\MH)$, and with respect to the trace norm $\ndot_tr$, respectively, the Hilbert-Schmidt norm $\ndot_HS$, they are complete ([ref:pro:operators_NOHS]). However, they are not $C^\ast$-algebras because $\norm{A}_HS^2 = \norm{A^\ast A}_tr$ for all $A \in \NO(\MH) \subset \HS(\MH)$.

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaConcreteCstar More generally, it holds that any uniformly closed $\ast$-subalgebra $\MFA \subset \BO(\MH)$ is a $C^\ast$-algebra, referred to as a . To see this, let $A \in \MFA$ be arbitrary. Then there exists a sequence $(A_n)_{n \in \N} \subset \MFA$ such that $\norm{A_n - A}_\mop \to 0$ as $n \to + \infty$. It follows from continuity of the multiplication and involution, and the $C^\ast$-property [ref:eq:operatorAlgebras_CStarProperty] that

$$
\norm{A^\ast A}_\mop = \lim_{n \to \infty} \norm{A_n^\ast A_n}_\mop = \lim_{n \to \infty} \norm{A_n}_\mop^2 = \norm{A}_\mop^2 \ . \tag*{\qedhere}
$$

### Positive Elements

In the following, the class of positive elements in a $C^\ast$-algebra will be introduced. It shall be assumed that all appearing algebras are considered over the field $\K = \C$ of complex numbers. Recall that the of an element $A \in \MFA$ of a unital $\C$-algebra is given by

$$
\sigma(A) \ce \set{\lambda \in \C \, : \, A - \lambda \idm \notin \GL(\MFA)} \ .
$$

## Definition: Positive element [label:def:operatorAlgebras_positiveElement]

Let $\MFA$ be a unital $\ast$-algebra. An element $A \in \MFA$ is called , denoted by $A \ge 0$, iff $A$ is self-adjoint and satisfies $\sigma(A) \subset [0, + \infty)$. The set of all positive elements will be denoted by the symbol $\PE{\MFA}$.

The following theorem characterizes the positive elements in a $C^\ast$-algebra. The proof can be found in [cite:BR1] or [cite:Conway85].

[Characterization of positive elements]#thm:operatorAlgebras_characterizationPE
Let $\MFA$ be a unital $C^\ast$-algebra. For an element $A \in \MFA$, the following assertions are equivalent:

[equiv]

- $A \in \PE{\MFA}$;

- there exists a unique $B \in \PE{\MFA}$ such that $A = B^2$;

- there exists $B \in \MFA$ such that $A = B^\ast B$.

[Self-dual convex cones]#para:operatorAlgebras_cones
Recall the following algebraic definitions [cite:SchaeferWolff99]: a in an $\R$-vector space $V$ is a subset $C \subset V$ which is closed under multiplication by non-negative scalars, , $x \in C, \, \lambda \ge 0 \, \implies \, \lambda x \in C$. The cone is called iff $\lambda, \mu \ge 0, \, x, y \in C \, \implies \, \lambda x + \mu y \in C$. For later use, introduce also the following notion [cite:SchaeferWolff99]: a cone $C \subset \MH$ in a Hilbert space $(\MH, \bdot)$ is called iff $C = \set{y \in \MH \, : \, \text{$ 0$ for all $x C$}}$.

## Proposition:

BR1]
Let $\MFA$ be a unital $C^\ast$-algebra. The set $\PE{\MFA}$ is a uniformly closed convex cone satisfying $\PE{\MFA} \cap (- \PE{\MFA}) = \{0\}$. Moreover, if $A \in \SE{\MFA}$, then the elements $A_\pm \ce \frac{1}{2} (\abs{A} \pm A)$ are positive, and they satisfy $A_+ A_- = 0$ and $A = A_+ - A_-$.

According to this result, the sum of two positive elements is again positive. Regarding the product of two such elements, the following property is found which will be needed later in [ref:ch:relativeEntropy].

## Lemma [label:lem:operatorAlgebras_productPositiveElements]

Let $\MFA$ be a unital $C^\ast$-algebra and $A, B \in \PE{\MFA}$. Then $AB \in \PE{\MFA}$ if and only if $AB = BA$.

## Proof

Assume first that $A$ and $B$ commute. Using [ref:thm:operatorAlgebras_characterizationPE], one can define the square root of a positive element $C \in \PE{\MFA}$: it is the unique element $\sqrt{C} \ce C^{1/2} \ce D \in \PE{\MFA}$ such that $D^2 = C$ [cite:BR1]. With this, the following decomposition holds true:

$$
AB = \sqrt{A} \sqrt{A} \sqrt{B} \sqrt{B} = \sqrt{B} \sqrt{A} \sqrt{A} \sqrt{B} = \bigl(\sqrt{B}\bigr)^\ast \bigl(\sqrt{A}\bigr)^\ast \sqrt{A} \sqrt{B} = \bigl(\sqrt{A} \sqrt{B}\bigr)^\ast \sqrt{A} \sqrt{B} \ .
$$

Note that $\sqrt{A}$ and $\sqrt{B}$ commute according to the assumption and the continuous functional calculus in $C^\ast$-algebras [cite:StratilaZsido19]. From [ref:thm:operatorAlgebras_characterizationPE], it now follows that $AB$ is a positive element.

Conversely, if $AB \ge 0$, then $\sigma(AB) \subset [0, + \infty)$ and $(AB)^\ast = AB$ by definition. But $(AB)^\ast = B^\ast A^\ast = BA$ since $A$ and $B$ are self-adjoint, hence $AB = BA$.

[Order relation for self-adjoint elements]#para:operatorAlgebras_orderSE
([cite:BR1])
Let $\MFA$ be a unital $C^\ast$-algebra. The closed convex cone $\PE{\MFA}$ induces an order structure on the real linear subspace $\SE{\MFA}$ of self-adjoint elements: for $A, B \in \SE{\MFA}$ define

$$
A \le B \quad \text{(or $B \ge A$)} \quad :\iff \quad B - A \in \PE{\MFA} \ .
$$

This relation defines a partial order on $\SE{\MFA}$: (1) it is clear that $A \le A$ for all $A \in \SE{\MFA}$ because $0 \in \PE{\MFA}$; (2) if $A, B \in \SE{\MFA}$ such that $A \le B$ and $B \le A$, it follows from [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_propertiesPE] that $B - A \in \PE{\MFA} \cap (- \PE{\MFA}) = \{0\}$, hence $B = A$; (3) finally, if there is a third element $C \in \SE{\MFA}$ such that $A \le B$ and $B \le C$, then $C - A = C - B + B - A$ is the sum of two positive elements, hence $C - A \ge 0$ as $\PE{\MFA}$ is a convex cone.

## Lemma [label:lem:operatorAlgebras_invertibleLowerBound]

Let $(\MFA, \idm)$ be a unital $C^\ast$-algebra and $A \in \PE{\MFA}$ be a positive element. Then $A$ is invertible if and only if there exists $\epsilon > 0$ such that $A \ge \epsilon \, \idm$.

## Proof

Assume that $A$ is invertible. From positivity of $A$, it follows that $\sigma(A) \subset [0, + \infty)$, and from invertibility of $A$, one can conclude that $0 \notin \sigma(A)$. Therefore, there exists $\epsilon > 0$ such that $\sigma(A) \subset [\epsilon, + \infty)$. Since $\sigma(A - \epsilon \, \idm) = \set{\lambda - \epsilon : \lambda \in \sigma(A)}$ [cite:BR1] and $\lambda \ge \epsilon$ for all $\lambda \in \sigma(A)$, it follows that $A - \epsilon \, \idm \ge 0$.

Conversely, assume that $A \ge \epsilon \, \idm$ for some $\epsilon > 0$. Employing an analogous argument as before, one obtains $\lambda \ge \epsilon$ for all $\lambda \in \sigma(A)$. Hence, $\sigma(A) \subset [\epsilon, + \infty)$, that is, $0 \notin \sigma(A)$, so $A$ must be invertible.

## Example: elements in $\BO(\MH)$ [label:exa:operatorAlgebras_positiveBO]

Let $(\MH, \bdot)$ be a Hilbert space and $\MFA = \BO(\MH)$ be the $C^\ast$-algebra of bounded linear operators on $\MH$ from [ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaBOCStar]. Then for all $A \in \MFA$, the following characterization holds true [cite:Conway85]:

$$
A \in \PE{\MFA} \quad \iff \quad \forall \xi \in \MH \, : \, \braket{\xi, A \xi} \ge 0 \ . \tag*{\qedhere}
$$

## Positive Linear Maps

#sec:operatorAlgebras_positiveMaps

Having introduced the closed convex cone $\PE{\MFA}$ of positive elements, now, a class of linear mappings between $C^\ast$-algebras shall be defined which preserve these cones.

### Basic Properties

## Definition: Positive mapping [label:def:operatorAlgebras_positiveMapping]

A linear mapping $f : \MFA \longto \MFB$ between two unital $C^\ast$-algebras $\MFA$ and $\MFB$ is called iff for every $A \in \MFA$, $A \ge 0$ implies $f(A) \ge 0$, that is, iff $f$ maps the cone $\PE{\MFA}$ into the cone $\PE{\MFB}$.

## Remark [label:rem:operatorAlgebras_positiveMappingOrderPreserving]

It follows immediately from this definition that positive linear mappings $f : \MFA \longto \MFB$ are order-preserving with respect to the order relation introduced in [ref:para:operatorAlgebras_orderSE]: if $A, B \in \SE{\MFA}$ satisfy $A \le B$, then $B - A \ge 0$ and hence $f(B) - f(A) \ge 0$ in $\MFB$, , $A \le B \implies f(A) \le f(B)$.

Next, it will be shown that positive mappings automatically satisfy an important algebraic property related to the algebra involution [cite:Stormer13].

## Proposition [label:pro:operatorAlgebras_positiveImpliesStarPreserving]

Let $f : \MFA \longto \MFB$ be a positive linear mapping between unital $C^\ast$-algebras $\MFA$ and $\MFB$. Then $f$ is $\ast$-preserving, , $f(A^\ast) = f(A)^\ast$ for all $A \in \MFA$.

## Proof

Any element $A \in \MFA$ can be written as $A = A_1 - A_2 + \ii (A_3 - A_4)$ for $\{A_i\}_{i=1}^{4} \subset \PE{\MFA}$ ( [ref:para:operatorAlgebras_astAlgebras] and [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_propertiesPE]). It holds that $A^\ast = A_1 - A_2 - \ii (A_3 - A_4)$ since positive elements are, by definition, self-adjoint. From positivity of $f$, it follows that $f(A_i) \in \PE{\MFB} \subset \SE{\MFB}$ for all $i \in \{1, \dotsc, 4\}$, hence linearity of $f$ implies $f(A^\ast) = f(A)^\ast$.

Positive mappings are also well-behaved in regards to the topological structure of the algebras: they are automatically continuous. A simple proof can be found in [cite:Paulsen03] or [cite:Stormer13].

## Proposition [label:pro:operatorAlgebras_positiveMappingContinuous]

Let $f : \MFA \longto \MFB$ be a positive linear mapping between unital $C^\ast$-algebras. Then $f$ is bounded with $\norm{f}_\mop \le 2 \norm{f(\idm)}_\MFB$.

### Completely Positive Maps

#subsec:operatorAlgebras_CP

For applications, one often requires mappings which satisfy a stronger positivity-preserving property than the one introduced in [ref:def:operatorAlgebras_positiveMapping]. (See, for example, [ref:sec:relativeEntropy_monotonicity].) These maps will be introduced in this subsection.

[Matrices over a $C^\ast$-algebra]#para:operatorAlgebras_matricesCStar
([cite:BlanchardBrüning15], [cite:Paulsen03])
Let $\MFA$ be a $C^\ast$-algebra and $n \in \N$ be arbitrary. Denote by $\Mat(n; \MFA)$ the space of all $(n \times n)$-matrices $A = [A_{ij}]$ with entries $A_{ij}$, $i, j \in \set{1, \dotsc, n}$, in the algebra $\MFA$; one also writes $A$ as

$$
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
A_{11} & \dots & A_{1n} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
A_{n1} & \dots & A_{nn}
\end{bmatrix} \ .
$$

It is clear that the space $\Mat(n; \MFA)$ is a $\ast$-algebra with respect to the usual matrix multiplication and involution, both being defined in terms of the respective algebraic operations on $\MFA$:

$$
[A_{ij}] [B_{ij}] \ce \biggl[\,\sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{ik} B_{kj}\biggr] \tand [A_{ij}]^\ast \ce [A_{ji}^\ast] \ .
$$

Furthermore, one can show that there exists a canonical algebra norm on $\Mat(n; \MFA)$ with respect to which this space becomes a $C^\ast$-algebra [cite:BR1], [cite:Takesaki79]. Finally, one can show that [cite:Conway00]

$$
\Mat(n; \MFA) = \MFA \otimes \Mat(n; \C) \ .
$$

Let $\MFB$ be another $C^\ast$-algebra and $f : \MFA \longto \MFB$ be a linear map. For all $n \in \N$, define linear mappings $f_{(n)} : \Mat(n; \MFA) \longto \Mat(n; \MFB)$ by setting for all $A = [A_{ij}] \in \Mat(n; \MFA)$:

[equation:eq:operatorAlgebras_nMatrixMap]
$$
f_{(n)}\bigl([A_{ij}]\bigr) \ce \bigl[f(A_{ij})\bigr] \ .
$$

## Definition: Completely positive mapping [label:def:operatorAlgebras_CP]

Let $f : \MFA \longto \MFB$ be a linear map between unital $C^\ast$-algebras $\MFA$ and $\MFB$. For some $n \in \N$, $f$ is called iff $f_{(n)} : \Mat(n; \MFA) \longto \Mat(n; \MFB)$ is a positive mapping in the sense of [ref:def:operatorAlgebras_positiveMapping]. Furthermore, $f$ is called iff for every $n \in \N$, $f_{(n)}$ is positive.

## Remark: interpretation [label:rem:operatorAlgebras_physicalInterpretationCP]

([cite:Lindblad75])
Consider a physical system $S_1$ described by a concrete $C^\ast$-algebra $\MFA \subset \BO(\MH_1)$ over a Hilbert space $\MH_1$, and let $S_2$ be a second system, independent of the system $S_1$, which is described by the algebra $\Mat(n; \C)$, $n \in \N$. According to the postulates of quantum mechanics [cite:Petz08], the Hilbert space for the combined system $S_1 + S_2$ is given by the Hilbert-space tensor product $\MH = \MH_1 \otimes \MH_2$, where $\dim(\MH_2) = n$.

Let $T : \MFA \longto \MFA$ be a linear mapping. By the duality between the bounded operators $\BO(\MH_1)$ and the trace-class operators $\NO(\MH_1)$, [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_sigmaWeakTopology] below, $T$ induces a linear mapping $T^\ast$ on the space $\NO(\MH_1)$ [cite:BlanchardBrüning15]. For $T^\ast$ to send quantum states of $S_1$ (that is, density matrices on $\MH_1$) again to quantum states, it is necessary that the mapping $T^\ast$ is positive.

Furthermore, under the assumption that $T$ does not influence the system $S_2$ directly, the mapping $T_{(n)} = T \otimes \id : \MFA \otimes \Mat(n; \C) \longto \MFA \otimes \Mat(n; \C)$, defined as in [ref:eq:operatorAlgebras_nMatrixMap], describes the resulting transformation on the combined system $S_1 + S_2$: $T_{(n)}(A_1 \otimes A_2) = T(A_1) \otimes A_2$. Therefore, in order for $(T_{(n)})^\ast$ to map quantum states of the combined system $S_1 + S_2$ to quantum states, $(T_{(n)})^\ast$ has to be positive, , $T^\ast$ has to be completely positive which is the case if and only if $T$ is completely positive [cite:BlanchardBrüning15].

#exa:operatorAlgebras_CP

[env]

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaConjugationCP Let $\MFA$ and $\MFB$ be unital $C^\ast$-algebras, let $f : \MFA \longto \C$ be a positive linear functional, let $\pi : \MFA \longto \MFB$ be a $\ast$-homomorphism, and let $\alpha : \MFA \longto \MFB$ be defined by $\alpha(A) \ce V^\ast \pi(A) V$ for some $V \in \MFB$. All of these three mappings are completely positive [cite:BlanchardBrüning15]. To show this, it suffices to check, according to [cite:BlanchardBrüning15], that for all $n \in \N$, $\{A_i\}_{i=1}^{n} \subset \MFA$, and $\{B_j\}_{j=1}^{n} \subset \MFB$, there holds $\sum_{i,j=1}^{n} B_i^\ast \alpha(A_i^\ast A_j) B_j \ge 0$ in the algebra $\MFB$. Indeed, for the mapping $\alpha$ one finds that

$$
\sum_{i,j=1}^{n} B_i^\ast \alpha(A_i^\ast A_j) B_j &= \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} B_i^\ast V^\ast \pi(A_i)^\ast \pi(A_j) V B_j = \sumbra{\bigg}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \pi(A_i) V B_i }^\ast \sumbra{\bigg}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \pi(A_j) V B_j}
$$

is a positive element in $\MFB$ by [ref:thm:operatorAlgebras_characterizationPE], hence $\alpha$ is completely positive.

- The notion of complete positivity can be used to distinguish between classical and quantum situations [cite:GustafsonSigal20], [cite:Keyl2002]: a positive mapping $f : \MFA \longto \MFB$ between $C^\ast$-algebras is automatically completely positive if either $\MFA$ or $\MFB$ is of the form $C^0(X; \K)$ for a compact Hausdorff space $X$ [cite:Paulsen03], [cite:Stormer13].

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaTrCP Let $\MFA$ be a unital $C^\ast$-algebra and $\tr : \Mat(n; \MFA) \longto \MFA$ be defined by $\tr([A_{ij}]) \ce \sum_{i=1}^{n} A_{ii}$. Then $\tr$ is a positive linear functional because for all $A = [A_{ij}] \in \Mat(n; \MFA)$, there holds

$$
\tr(A^\ast A) = \tr\Biggl(\biggl[\,\sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{ki}^\ast A_{kj}\biggr]\Biggr) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{ki}^\ast A_{ki} \ge 0
$$

since $A_{ki}^\ast A_{ki} \ge 0$ in $\MFA$ for all $i, k \in \set{1, \dotsc, n}$ ([ref:thm:operatorAlgebras_characterizationPE]) and $\PE{\MFA}$ is a convex cone ([ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_propertiesPE]). One can show that $\tr$ is actually completely positive [cite:Paulsen03].

- Let $\MH_1$ and $\MH_2$ be two Hilbert spaces and $\MH \ce \MH_1 \otimes \MH_2$. Define a mapping $\alpha : \BO(\MH_1) \longto \BO(\MH)$, $A \longmto A \otimes \id_{\MH_2}$, which is completely positive [cite:Petz08]. Its dual map $\alpha^\ast : \NO(\MH) \longto \NO(\MH_1)$, in the sense discussed in [ref:rem:operatorAlgebras_physicalInterpretationCP], is the so-called partial trace $\alpha^\ast(A \otimes B) = A \tr(B)$ which is physically very relevant [cite:Petz08]. By [cite:BlanchardBrüning15], $\alpha^\ast$ is completely positive.

- Consider the $(2 \times 2)$-matrices $\MFA = \Mat(2; \C)$ and the transposition $f : \MFA \longto \MFA$, $A \longmto A^T$. This is a positive mapping: for all $A \in \MFA$, it holds that

$$
f(A^\ast A) = (A^\ast A)^T = A^T (A^\ast)^T = A^T (A^T)^\ast \ge 0 \ .
$$

However, $f$ fails to be 2-positive [cite:HiaiPetz14]. To see this, consider the following element of the algebra $\Mat(2; \MFA) = \Mat(2; \C) \otimes \Mat(2; \C) = \Mat(4; \C)$:

$$
A \ce \bmat{\pmat{2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1} & \pmat{0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0} \\ \pmat{0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0} & \pmat{1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2}} = \bmat{2 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 2} \ .
$$

Its eigenvalues are $\sigma(A) = \set{4, 2, 0}$ (the last eigenvalue appears twice), hence it is positive. Yet,

$$
f_{(2)}(A) = \bmat{\pmat{2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1} & \pmat{0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0} \\ \pmat{0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0} & \pmat{1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2}} = \bmat{2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 2}
$$

has eigenvalues $\sigma(f_2(A)) = \set{3, 1, -1}$ (the first eigenvalue appears twice), , it is not a positive element in $\Mat(2; \MFA)$. One can even show that for all $n > 1$, $f_{(n)}$ is not positive [cite:Conway00].

The following result of [cite:Choi80] characterizes 2-positive mappings.

## Proposition [label:pro:operatorAlgebras_2positivity]

Let $f : \MFA \longto \MFB$ be a positive linear mapping between two unital $C^\ast$-algebras, and suppose that $f(\idm_\MFA) \in \PE{\MFB} \cap \GL(\MFB)$ is positive and invertible. Furthermore, let $R, S, T \in \MFA$ be arbitrary with $T \in \PE{\MFA} \cap \GL(\MFA)$. Then the following properties are equivalent:

[equiv]

- $f$ is 2-positive;

- If $R \ge S \inv{T} S^\ast$ in $\MFA$, then $f(R) \ge f(S) f(T)^{-1} f(S)^\ast$ in $\MFB$;

- $f(S \inv{T} S^\ast) \ge f(S) f(T)^{-1} f(S)^\ast$ in $\MFB$.

### Schwarz Mappings

To conclude this section, another class of positive mappings between $C^\ast$-algebras is introduced which will be of particular relevance for the study of monotonicity of the relative entropy in [ref:sec:relativeEntropy_monotonicity]. The following definition subscribes to the convention of [cite:OP04].

## Definition: Schwarz map [label:def:operatorAlgebras_SchwarzMap]

Let $(\MFA, \idm_\MFA)$ and $(\MFB, \idm_\MFB)$ be two unital $C^\ast$-algebras. A linear mapping $\alpha : \MFA \longto \MFB$ is called a iff $\alpha$ is unital, that is, $\alpha(\idm_\MFA) = \idm_\MFB$, and satisfies for all $A \in \MFA$ the following inequality, referred to as :

$$
\alpha(A)^\ast \alpha(A) \le \alpha(A^\ast A) \ .
$$

## Lemma [label:lem:operatorAlgebras_basicPropertiesSchwarzMap]

Every Schwarz mapping $\alpha : \MFA \longto \MFB$ is positive and satisfies the inequality $\alpha(A) \alpha(A)^\ast \le \alpha(A A^\ast)$ for all $A \in \MFA$.

## Proof

Let $A = B^\ast B$, $B \in \MFA$, be an arbitrary positive element in the $C^\ast$-algebra $\MFA$ ( [ref:thm:operatorAlgebras_characterizationPE]). Then $\alpha(A) = \alpha(B^\ast B) \ge \alpha(B)^\ast \alpha(B) \ge 0$ in $\MFB$ by [ref:eq:operatorAlgebras_SchwarzInequality].

Since $\MFA$ is closed under the algebra involution, one can choose $A^\ast$ in [ref:eq:operatorAlgebras_SchwarzInequality] to obtain $\alpha(A^\ast)^\ast \alpha(A^\ast) \le \alpha(A A^\ast)$. As was just shown, $\alpha$ is a positive mapping, hence it is especially $\ast$-preserving by [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_positiveImpliesStarPreserving]. This proves the asserted inequality.

According to [ref:lem:operatorAlgebras_basicPropertiesSchwarzMap], Schwarz mappings are stronger than positive mappings. Similarly, the next proposition shows that 2-positive mappings are stronger than Schwarz mappings; the proof can be found in [cite:Paulsen03].

## Proposition [label:pro:operatorAlgebras_2PmapsAreSchwarzMaps]

Let $\MFA$ and $\MFB$ be two unital $C^\ast$-algebras, and let $\alpha : \MFA \longto \MFB$ be a unital 2-positive mapping. Then $\alpha$ satisfies the Schwarz inequality [ref:eq:operatorAlgebras_SchwarzInequality].

## von Neumann Algebras

#sec:operatorAlgebras_vonNeumann

In [ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaConcreteCstar], the notion of a concrete $C^\ast$-algebra was defined to be a uniformly closed $\ast$-subalgebra of $\BO(\MH)$. Considering further classes of $\ast$-subalgebras of $\BO(\MH)$ which satisfy stronger closure conditions leads to the concept of von Neumann algebras.

### Operator Topologies

Let $(\MH, \bdot)$ be a Hilbert space and $\ndot$ be the norm on $\MH$ induced by $\bdot$. In the following, three important locally convex topologies on $\BO(\MH)$ shall be defined by specifying a family of semi-norms ( [ref:pro:topologicalVectorSpaces_LCS]). The definitions can be found in [cite:BlanchardBrüning15], [cite:BR1], or [cite:StratilaZsido19].

[Strong topology]#para:operatorAlgebras_strongTop
For $\xi \in \MH$, the mapping $A \longmto \norm{A \xi}$ on $\BO(\MH)$ is clearly a semi-norm. The topology $\MFT_{so} \ce \MFT_{P_{so}}$ induced by the system $P_{so} \ce \set{p_\xi : \xi \in \MH}$ of semi-norms

$$
p_\xi(A) \ce \norm{A \xi} \com A \in \BO(\MH) \ ,
$$

is called the (also: ) on $\BO(\MH)$. Since by [ref:pro:topologicalVectorSpaces_LCS] a net $(A_i)_{i \in I} \subset \BO(\MH)$ converges to an operator $A \in \BO(\MH)$ with respect to $\MFT_{so}$ if and only if $\lim_{i \in I} p_x(A_i - A) = \lim_{i \in I} \norm{(A_i - A) \xi} \to 0$ for all $\xi \in \MH$, it follows that the strong operator topology is the topology of pointwise convergence on $\BO(\MH)$.

[Weak topology]#para:operatorAlgebras_weakTop
For $\xi, \eta \in \MH$, the mapping $A \longmto \abs{\braket{\xi, A \eta}}$ on $\BO(\MH)$ is a semi-norm. The topology $\MFT_{wo} \ce \MFT_{P_{wo}}$ induced by the family $P_{wo} \ce \set{p_{\xi,\eta} : \xi, \eta \in \MH}$, where

$$
p_{\xi, \eta}(A) \ce \abs{\braket{\xi, A \eta}} \com A \in \BO(\MH) \ ,
$$

is called the (also: ) on $\BO(\MH)$. As for the strong operator topology, it follows from [ref:pro:topologicalVectorSpaces_LCS] that the weak operator topology is the topology of pointwise weak convergence on $\BO(\MH)$.

[$\sigma$-weak topology]#para:operatorAlgebras_sigmaWeakTop
Introduce the notation

$$
\ell^2(\N; \MH) \ce \set[\Bigg]{(\xi_n)_{n \in \N} \ : \ \xi_n \in \MH, \, \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \norm{\xi_n}^2 < + \infty}
$$

for the space of all sequences $(\xi_n)_{n \in \N} \subset \MH$ which are square-summable, , $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \norm{\xi_n}^2 < + \infty$.

Let $(\xi_n)_{n \in \N}, (\eta_n)_{n \in \N} \in \ell^2(\N; \MH)$ be arbitrary. For every $A \in \BO(\MH)$, it follows by using first the Cauchy-Schwarz and then Hölder's inequality that [cite:BR1]

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \abs{\braket{\xi_n, A \eta_n}} \le \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \norm{A}_\mop \norm{\xi_n} \norm{\eta_n} \le \norm{A}_\mop \sumbra{\Bigg}{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \norm{\xi_n}^2}^{1/2} \sumbra{\Bigg}{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \norm{\eta_n}^2}^{1/2} < + \infty \ .
$$

This shows that $A \longmto \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \abs{\braket{\xi_n, A \eta_n}}$ is a semi-norm on $\BO(\MH)$. The topology $\MFT_{uw} \ce \MFT_{P_{uw}}$ induced by the system $P_{uw} \ce \set[\big]{q_{(\xi_n), (\eta_n)} : (\xi_n)_{n \in \N}, (\eta_n)_{n \in \N} \in \ell^2(\N; \MH)}$ of semi-norms

$$
q_{(\xi_n), (\eta_n)}(A) \ce \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \abs{\braket{\xi_n, A \eta_n}} \com A \in \BO(\MH) \ ,
$$

is called the (or: ; ). It holds that the mappings $A \longmto A B$ and $A \longmto B A$ on $\BO(\MH)$ for fixed $B \in \BO(\MH)$, as well as the mapping $A \longmto A^\ast$, are continuous with respect to both $\MFT_{uw}$ and $\MFT_{wo}$ [cite:BR1].

The next proposition characterizes the $\sigma$-weak topology in terms of trace-class operators. For proofs of the assertions, see [cite:BlanchardBrüning15] and [cite:BR1].

## Proposition: $\sigma$-weak topology and $\NO(\MH)$ [label:pro:operatorAlgebras_sigmaWeakTopology]

It holds that $\cdual{\bigl(\NO(\MH), \ndot_tr\bigr)} \cong \bigl(\BO(\MH), \ndot_\mop\bigr)$ with respect to the duality mapping

$$
\Phi :
\begin{cases}
\begin{aligned}
\BO(\MH) &\longto \cdual{\NO(\MH)} \ , \\
A &\longmto \bigl(\Phi_A : \rho \longmto \tr(A \rho)\bigr) \ .
\end{aligned}
\end{cases}
$$

The weak-$\ast$ topology $\sigma\bigl(\BO(\MH), \NO(\MH)\bigr) = \sigma\bigl(\cdual{\NO(\MH)}, \NO(\MH)\bigr)$ on $\BO(\MH)$ arising from the above duality, , the topology generated by the semi-norms $p_\rho(A) \ce \abs{\tr(A \rho)}$, $\rho \in \NO(\MH)$, on $\BO(\MH)$ ( [ref:para:topologicalVectorSpaces_weakStar]) coincides with the $\sigma$-weak operator topology:

$$
\MFT_{uw} = \sigma\bigl(\BO(\MH), \NO(\MH)\bigr) \ .
$$

In particular, for every $\omega \in \cdual{\bigl(\BO(\MH), \MFT_{uw}\bigr)}$, there exist sequences $(\xi_n)_{n \in \N}, (\eta_n)_{n \in \N} \in \ell^2(\N; \MH)$, equivalently, a trace-class operator $\rho \in \NO(\MH)$, such that

$$
\omega = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \braket{\xi_n, \, \sbullet \ \eta_n} \com \text{equivalently} \com \omega = \tr(\rho \ \sbullet\,) \ .
$$

The different topologies introduced in [ref:para:operatorAlgebras_strongTop], [ref:para:operatorAlgebras_weakTop] and [ref:para:operatorAlgebras_sigmaWeakTop] are in the following relation ( [ref:para:topologicalVectorSpaces_comparisonTopologies]) to one another [cite:BlanchardBrüning15], [cite:BR1].

## Proposition [label:pro:operatorAlgebras_comparisonTopologies]

The following relations hold true:

$$
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large]
\MFT_{wo} \arrow[draw=none]{r}[sloped,auto=false]{\le} \arrow[draw=none]{d}[sloped,auto=false]{\le} & \MFT_{so} \arrow[draw=none]{d}[sloped,auto=false]{\le} \\
\MFT_{uw} \arrow[draw=none]{r}[sloped,auto=false]{\le} & \MFT_{norm}
\end{tikzcd}
$$

### Definition, Bicommutant Theorem, Examples

## Definition: von Neumann algebra [label:def:operatorAlgebras_vonNeumann]

Let $\MH$ be a Hilbert space. A $\ast$-subalgebra of operators $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ which contains the identity $\id_\MH$ and which is closed in the strong operator topology is called a This terminology was introduced by in 1957 [cite:Dixmier81]. In the works of [cite:vonNeumann30] (and \& [cite:MurrayVonNeumann36]), they were called . (or: concrete $W^\ast$-algebra).

## Remark [label:rem:operatorAlgebras_vonNeumann]

From Mazur's theorem [cite:Voigt20], it follows that a von Neumann algebra is also closed with respect to the weak operator topology. Furthermore, since $\MFT_{so} \subset \MFT_norm$ by [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_comparisonTopologies], it holds that $\MFM$ is uniformly closed as well, [ref:para:topologicalVectorSpaces_comparisonTopologies], and hence every von Neumann algebra is a concrete $C^\ast$-algebra according to [ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaConcreteCstar].

## Definition: Commutant [label:def:operatorAlgebras_commutant]

For a subset $\MFA \subset \BO(\MH)$, the is defined to be the set

$$
\comm{\MFA} \ce \set{A \in \BO(\MH) \ : \ \text{$A B = B A$ for all $B \in \MFA$}}
$$

of all bounded linear operators which commute with every element from the set $\MFA$. Similarly, the (or: double commutant) of $\MFA$ is defined as $\bicomm{\MFA} \ce \comm{(\comm{\MFA})}$.

## Lemma:

Moretti19]
Let $\MFA \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a subset. Then $\comm{\MFA}$ is a strongly closed, unital subalgebra of $\BO(\MH)$. If $\MFA$ is self-adjoint, then $\comm{\MFA}$ is even a von Neumann algebra.

The next theorem is one of the most important and deep results in the theory of von Neumann algebras. It was discovered by in 1930 [cite:vonNeumann30], and a modern proof can be found in [cite:BR1], [cite:Moretti19], or [cite:StratilaZsido19].

[von Neumann's bicommutant theorem]#thm:operatorAlgebras_bicommutant
Let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a $\ast$-subalgebra which contains the identity $\id_\MH$. Then the following assertions are equivalent:

[equiv]

- $\MFM$ is a von Neumann algebra;

- $\MFM$ is weakly closed;

- $\MFM$ is $\sigma$-weakly closed;

- $\MFM = \bicomm{\MFM}$.

#exa:operatorAlgebras_vonNeumann

[env]

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaLInf Let $(X, \Sigma, \mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure space. Consider the Hilbert space $\MH = L^2(X, \mu)$ and the $C^\ast$-algebra $\MFM = L^\infty(X, \mu)$ from [ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaLInfCStar]. One can view $\MFM$ as a $\ast$-subalgebra of $\BO(\MH)$ by virtue of the identification $\MFM \owns f \longmto M_f \in \BO(\MH)$, where $M_f g \ce f g$, $g \in \MH$, is the multiplication operator with the function $f$; that is, one identities

$$
\MFM \cong \set[\big]{M_f \in \BO(\MH) \ : \ f \in L^\infty(X, \mu)} \ .
$$

In this identification, $\MFM$ becomes a von Neumann algebra acting on $\MH$. This can be proved by showing that $\comm{\MFM} \subset \MFM$, see [cite:Conway85], [cite:Conway00], or [cite:StratilaZsido19] for detailed arguments.

The $C^\ast$-algebra of continuous functions $\MFA = C^0(X; \K)$ from [ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaCCStar], which, for $X$ a compact topological space, can also be viewed as $\MFA \subset \BO(\MH)$ in terms of the above identification, does not form a von Neumann algebra because $\MFA$ is only uniformly, but neither strongly nor weakly closed in $\BO(\MH)$ [cite:KadisonRingrose97]. ($L^\infty$-functions are pointwise almost-everywhere limits of continuous functions.)

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaBOvN Let $\MH$ be a Hilbert space. Then the $C^\ast$-algebra $\BO(\MH)$ from [ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaBOCStar] is a von Neumann algebra since $\comm{\BO(\MH)} = \C \cdot \id_\MH$ and $\comm{\{\C \cdot \id_\MH\}} = \BO(\MH)$, hence $\bicomm{\BO(\MH)} = \BO(\MH)$. To see this, note that if $A \in \comm{\BO(\MH)}$, then $A$ commutes, in particular, with every one-dimensional projection $P_\xi = \braket{\xi, \,\sbullet\ } \, \xi$, $\xi \in \MH$. This implies that there exists a constant $\alpha \in \C$ such that $A \xi = \alpha \xi$. Since $A$ is linear, it follows for all $\xi, \eta \in \MH$ that $A(\xi + \eta) = \alpha \xi + \beta \eta$ for some $\alpha, \beta \in \C$, but one also has $A(\xi + \eta) = \gamma (\xi + \eta)$ for $\gamma \in \C$, hence one may conclude $\alpha = \beta = \gamma$, that is, $A = \alpha \, \id_\MH$.

The $C^\ast$-algebra of compact operators $\KO(\MH)$ from [ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaKOCStar] is not a von Neumann algebra because $\comm{\KO(\MH)} = \C \cdot \id_\MH$ as before, and hence $\bicomm{\KO(\MH)} = \BO(\MH)$. This follows since finite-rank operators are compact, and they are dense in $\BO(\MH)$.

Many applications in mathematical physics require working with unbounded operators (see, for example, [ref:ch:perturbationTheory]). Due to the flexibility of von Neumann algebras, it turns out that one can affiliate unbounded operators with this class of $C^\ast$-algebras.

## Definition: Affiliated operator [label:def:operatorAlgebras_affiliatedElement]

Let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a von Neumann algebra. A closed linear operator $T : \MH \supset \dom(T) \longto \MH$ on $\MH$ ([ref:def:operators_closed]) is said to be , and the set of these operators is denoted by $\AE{\MFM}$, iff for all $\comm{A} \in \comm{\MFM}$ it holds that

$$
\comm{A} \bigl(\dom(T)\bigr) \subset \dom(T) \tand \comm{A} T \subset T \comm{A} \ .
$$

Essentially, a closed operator $T$ is affiliated with a von Neumann algebra $\MFM$ if and only if $T$ strongly commutes [cite:Moretti19] with the elements of the commutant $\comm{\MFM}$. The next important result shows that the above definition is somewhat natural [cite:DJP03].

## Proposition [label:pro:operatorAlgebras_characterizationAffiliation]

Let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a von Neumann algebra and $T : \MH \supset \dom(T) \longto \MH$ be self-adjoint. It holds that $T \in \AE{\MFM}$ if and only if all bounded Borel functions of $T$ belong to the algebra $\MFM$.

### Cyclic and Separating Vectors

The concept of a cyclic and separating vector $\xi \in \MH$ for a von Neumann algebra $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ is of great importance for the theory and will be used extensively in the following three chapters.

[Closed subspaces and projections]#para:operatorAlgebras_closedSubspaceProjection
For arbitrary subsets $\MFA \subset \BO(\MH)$ and $\MK \subset \MH$, introduce the following notation:

$$
\MFA \MK \ce \lin_\K \set{A \xi \, : \, A \in \MFA,\, \xi \in \MK} \tand [\MFA \MK] \ce \clos_{\ndot} (\MFA \MK) \ .
$$

By the correspondence between orthogonal projections and closed subspaces ([ref:rem:operators_orthogonalProjectionClosedSubspace]), there exists a unique orthogonal projection $P \in \PO(\MH)$ onto $[\MFA \MK]$. Often, the projection $P$ will also be denoted by the symbol $[\MFA \MK]$. In case that $\MK = \{\xi\}$ for some $\xi \in \MH$, one writes $\MFA \MK \equiv \MFA \xi$ and $[\MFA \MK] \equiv [\MFA \xi]$.

## Definition: Cyclic and separating vectors [label:def:operatorAlgebras_cyclicSeparating]

Let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a von Neumann algebra. A set of vectors $\MS \subset \MH$ is said to be for the algebra $\MFM$ iff $[\MFM \MS] = \MH$, that is, if the subspace generated by $\MFM \MS$ lies dense in $\MH$ with respect to the norm topology. The set $\MS$ is called for $\MFM$ iff for every $A \in \MFM$, $A \xi = 0$ for all $\xi \in \MS$ implies that $A = 0$.

## Proposition [label:pro:operatorAlgebras_cyclicSeparating]

Let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a von Neumann algebra and $\MS \subset \MH$ be a subset.

- $\MS$ is cyclic for $\MFM$ if and only if $\MS$ is separating for $\comm{\MFM}$.

- $\MS$ is separating for $\MFM$ if and only if $\MS$ is cyclic for $\comm{\MFM}$.

## Proof

[ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_cyclicMseparatingCommM]. [cite:BR1] Assume first that $\MS$ is cyclic for $\MFM$. Let $\comm{A} \in \comm{\MFM}$ be arbitrary such that for every $\xi \in \MS$, $\comm{A} \xi = 0$. For all $A \in \MFM$, it follows that $ \comm{A} A \xi = A \comm{A} \xi = 0$, and hence $\comm{A} [\MFM \MS] = 0$ by linearity and continuity of $\comm{A}$. Since $[\MFM \MS] = \MH$ by assumption, one can conclude $\comm{A} = 0$ which shows that $\MS$ is separating for $\comm{\MFM}$.

Conversely, assume that for every $\comm{A} \in \comm{\MFM}$ which satisfies $\comm{A} \xi = 0$ for all $\xi \in \MS$, it follows that $\comm{A} = 0$. Let $P \ce [\MFM \MS] \in \PO(\MH)$, then the claim $[\MFM \MS] = \MH$ is equivalent to the operator identity $P = \id_\MH$, see [ref:cor:operators_characterizationPerp] [ref:enu:operators_densePerp]. On the set $\MS$, it clearly holds that $\id_\MH - P = 0$ since $\id_\MH \in \MFM$ and hence $\MS \subset [\MFM \MS]$. Moreover, $P \in \comm{\MFM}$ [cite:BR1]: for all $A \in \MFM$ and $\eta \in \MH$, one has $A P \eta \in [\MFM \MS]$ by definition of this space, hence $A P = P A P$ ([ref:lem:operators_rangeProjection]). This gives $P A = (A^\ast P)^\ast = (P A^\ast P)^\ast = P A P = A P$. Therefore, it follows that $\id_\MH - P \in \comm{\MFM}$ by [ref:lem:operatorAlgebras_propComm] which, together with the previous observation and the assumption, implies that $P = \id_\MH$.

[ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_separatingMcyclicCommM]. If $\MS$ is separating for the algebra $\MFM$, it is for $\bicomm{\MFM}$ as well by [ref:thm:operatorAlgebras_bicommutant]. Using assertion [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_cyclicMseparatingCommM] together with the fact that $\comm{\MFM}$ is a von Neumann algebra ([ref:lem:operatorAlgebras_propComm]), it follows that $\MS$ is cyclic for $\comm{\MFM}$. Conversely, if $\MS$ is cyclic for $\comm{\MFM}$, it is separating for $\bicomm{\MFM}$ by [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_cyclicMseparatingCommM], and hence also for $\MFM$.

[Cyclic projections]#para:operatorAlgebras_cyclicProjections
Let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a von Neumann algebra and $\xi \in \MH$ be arbitrary. Projections of the form $P_\xi \ce [\comm{\MFM} \xi]$ and $\comm{P}_\xi \ce [\MFM \xi]$ are called . It holds that $P_\xi \in \MFM$ and $\comm{P}_\xi \in \comm{\MFM}$. Indeed, in the proof of [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_cyclicSeparating], it was already shown that $\comm{P}_\xi \in \comm{\MFM}$. Therefore, it also follows that $P_\xi = [\comm{\MFM} \xi] \in \bicomm{\MFM} = \MFM$.

A vector $\xi \in \MH$ is cyclic for the algebra $\MFM$ if and only if $\comm{P}_\xi = \id_\MH$, and it is separating for $\MFM$ if and only if $P_\xi = \id_\MH$. This can be seen as follows: $\xi$ is cyclic for $\MFM$ $\iff$ $[\MFM \xi] = \MH$ $\iff$ $\comm{P}_\xi = \id_\MH$ according to [ref:cor:operators_characterizationPerp] [ref:enu:operators_densePerp]. Similarly, $\xi$ is separating for $\MFM$ $\iff$ $\xi$ is separating for $\bicomm{\MFM}$ $\iff$ $\xi$ is cyclic for $\comm{\MFM}$ $\iff$ $[\comm{\MFM} \xi] = \MH$ $\iff$ $P_\xi = \id_\MH$ by [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_cyclicSeparating].

## States and Representations

#sec:operatorAlgebras_representationsStates

The goal of this section is to argue that every abstract $C^\ast$-algebra can be realized as a subalgebra of $\BO(\MH)$ for a suitable Hilbert space $\MH$. To this end, the important notions of a state on a $C^\ast$-algebra and a normal state on a von Neumann algebra will be introduced and studied in some detail. The former will be employed in the so-called GNS-representation of a $C^\ast$-algebra.

### General States on a $C^\ast$-Algebra

General States on a C*-Algebra

## Definition: State [label:def:operatorAlgebras_state]

Let $(\MFA, \idm)$ be a unital $C^\ast$-algebra. A linear functional $\omega : \MFA \longto \C$ is called a iff it is positive and $\omega(\idm) = 1$. The set of all states on the algebra $\MFA$ will be denoted by the symbol $\SS(\MFA)$. If, for every $A \in \MFA$, $\omega(A^\ast A) = 0$ implies $A = 0$, then the state $\omega$ is called .

The following proposition contains fundamental properties of positive linear functionals on $C^\ast$-algebras. Its proof can be found, for example, in [cite:BärFredenhagen09] or [cite:BR1].

## Proposition [label:pro:operatorAlgebras_formFromState]

Let $\MFA$ be a $C^\ast$-algebra and $\omega : \MFA \longto \C$ be a positive linear functional. Then the mapping $\MFq_\omega : \MFA \times \MFA \longto \C$, $\MFq_\omega(A, B) \ce \omega(A^\ast B)$, is a positive semi-definite Hermitian sesquilinear form on $\MFA$. In particular, it satisfies the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality:

$$
\forall A, B \in \MFA \ : \ \abs{\omega(A^\ast B)}^2 \le \omega(A^\ast A) \, \omega(B^\ast B) \ .
$$

#exa:operatorAlgebras_states

[env]

- Let $n \in \N$ and $\MFA = \Mat(n; \C)$ from [ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaMatCStar]. Consider the trace functional $\tr : \MFA \longto \C$, $A \longmto \tr(A)$, which was shown to be a positive mapping in [ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CP] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaTrCP]. A corresponding state $\tau : \MFA \longto \C$ can be obtained by setting $\tau(A) \ce \frac{1}{n} \tr(A)$ for all $A \in \MFA$.

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaMeasureState Let $(X, \MFT)$ be a compact Hausdorff space, let $\MFA = C^0(X; \C)$ be the $C^\ast$-algebra of continuous functions on $X$ ([ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaCCStar]), and let $\mu$ be a measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\MB(X)$ of $X$ (that is, the smallest $\sigma$-algebra containing $\MFT$). Define a functional $\omega_\mu : \MFA \longto \C$ by

$$
\omega_\mu(f) \ce \int\nolimits_X f \diff \mu \quad (f \in \MFA) \ .
$$

From the properties of the $\mu$-integral, it follows that $\omega_\mu$ is positive ($f \ge 0 \, \implies \, \int_X f \diff \mu \ge 0$). Furthermore, if $\mu$ is a probability measure, , $\mu(X) = 1$, then $\omega_\mu$ is a state on $\MFA$.

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaVectorFunctional Let $\MFA \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a unital concrete $C^\ast$-algebra ([ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaConcreteCstar]) and $\Omega \in \MH$ be a vector. Define a functional $\omega_\Omega : \MFA \longto \C$ by

$$
\omega_\Omega(A) \ce \braket{\Omega, A \Omega} \quad (A \in \MFA) \ .
$$

This functional is positive since for all $A \in \MFA$, it holds that $\omega_\Omega(A^\ast A) = \braket{A \Omega, A \Omega} = \norm{A \Omega}^2 \ge 0$. One refers to $\omega_\Omega$ as the induced by the vector $\Omega$. If $\norm{\Omega} = 1$, then it follows that $\omega_\Omega(\id_\MH) = 1$, hence $\omega_\Omega$ defines a state on $\MFA$.

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaNormalState Let $\MH$ be a separable Hilbert space, let $\MFA = \BO(\MH)$ ([ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_CStar] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaBOCStar]), and let $\rho \in \PE{\NO(\MH)}$ be a positive trace-class operator. Defining $\omega_\rho : \MFA \longto \C$ by

$$
\omega_\rho(A) \ce \tr(\rho A) \quad (A \in \MFA)
$$

yields a positive linear functional: $\omega_\rho(A^\ast A) = \tr(\rho A^\ast A) = \tr(\rho^{1/2} A^\ast A \rho^{1/2}) \ge 0$ due to cyclicity and positivity of the trace. Furthermore, if $\rho$ is a density matrix ([ref:def:operators_densityMatrix]), ,
$\tr(\rho) = 1$, then $\omega_\rho$ is a state on $\MFA$. States of this form are called . One can show that $\omega_\rho$ is faithful if and only if $\rho$ is invertible [cite:BR1].

If $\dim(\MH) < + \infty$, then every state on $\BO(\MH)$ is induced by a density matrix, , $\SS(\BO(\MH)) = \DM(\MH)$ [cite:Landsman17]. This is no longer true if $\dim(\MH) = + \infty$, see [cite:Landsman17].

### Normal States on a von Neumann Algebra

#subsec:operatorAlgebras_normalStates

In this subsection, normal states defined on an arbitrary von Neumann algebra will be investigated more closely.

## Definition: Normal functional [label:def:operatorAlgebras_normalState]

Let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a von Neumann algebra and $\pdual{\MFM} \ce \cdual{(\MFM, \MFT_{uw})}$ be the set of all $\sigma$-weakly continuous linear functionals. A positive element of $\pdual{\MFM}$ is called a , and the set of all these is denoted by the symbol $\NF{\MFM}$. A normal functional $\omega$ satisfying $\omega(\id_\MH) = 1$ is called a , and the set of these is denoted $\NS(\MFM)$.

## Proposition:
Let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a von Neumann algebra. The space $\pdual{\MFM}$ is a Banach space with respect to the operator norm, and $\MFM$ is the dual of $\pdual{\MFM}$ with respect to the duality $\MFM \times \pdual{\MFM} \owns (A, \omega) \longto \omega(A) \in \C$, that is, $\MFM = \cdual{(\pdual{\MFM})}$.

[env]

- The previous assertion establishes that every von Neumann algebra possesses a . Generally, an abstract $C^\ast$-algebra which possesses a predual space is called a .
The terminology was also introduced by in 1951 [cite:Segal51b].
It was shown by in 1956 that every $W^\ast$-algebra is a von Neumann algebra [cite:Sakai56], [cite:Sakai98], hence these two notions are actually equivalent.

- Let $\omega \in \pdual{\MFM}$ be $\sigma$-weakly continuous. From [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_comparisonTopologies] and [ref:para:topologicalVectorSpaces_comparisonTopologies], it follows that $\omega \in \cdual{\MFM}$. Furthermore, characterization of continuity in a locally convex space [cite:Werner18] and the Hahn-Banach theorem [cite:Werner18] imply that $\omega$ can be extended to a $\sigma$-weakly continuous linear functional on $\BO(\MH)$ so that [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_sigmaWeakTopology] applies [cite:BR1].

The next important result gives a characterization of normal states. Proofs of the assertions can be found in [cite:BR1], [cite:StratilaZsido19], and [cite:Takesaki79].

[Characterization of normal states]#thm:operatorAlgebras_characterizationNormalStates
Let $\omega \in \SS(\MFM)$. The following assertions are equivalent:

[equiv]

- $\omega$ is normal;

- there exist a sequence $(\xi_n)_{n \in \N} \in \ell^2(\N; \MH)$ such that $\omega = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \braket{\xi_n, \,\sbullet\ \xi_n}$;

- there exists a density matrix $\rho \in \DM(\MH)$ such that $\omega = \tr(\rho \ \sbullet\,)$;

- for every increasing net $(A_i)_{i \in I} \subset \PE{\MFM}$ with an upper bound (with respect to the order relation from [ref:para:operatorAlgebras_orderSE]), there holds $\omega\bigl(\sup_{i \in I} A_i\bigr) = \sup_{i \in I} \omega(A_i)$.

#exa:operatorAlgebras_normalStates

[env]

- #enu:operatorAlgebras_exaNormalStateAbelian Let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a commutative von Neumann algebra on a separable Hilbert space $\MH$. According to a theorem of [cite:Segal51b, Segal51], there is a compact Hausdorff space $X$ and a measure $\mu$ on $\bigl(X, \MB(X)\bigr)$ such that $\MH \cong L^2(X, \mu)$ and $\MFM \cong L^\infty(X, \mu)$ [cite:Conway85], [cite:Dixmier81], [cite:Sakai98]. Since $\cdual{L^1(X, \mu)} = L^\infty(X, \mu)$ [cite:Werner18], it follows that the predual space of $\MFM$ is given by $\pdual{\MFM} = L^1(X, \mu)$. Explicitly, a function $h \in L^1(X, \mu)$ gives rise to the measure $\diff \nu \ce h \diff \mu$ which induces the functional $\omega_\nu(f) = \int_X f \diff \nu$, $f \in \MFM$ ([ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_states] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaMeasureState]). If, additionally, $h$ is assumed to be non-negative, then one can define $g \ce \sqrt{h} \in \MH$ to obtain

$$
\omega_\nu(f) = \int\nolimits_X f h \diff \mu = \int\nolimits_X \ol{g} f g \diff \mu = \braket{g, f g} = \omega_g(f) \ ,
$$

that is, $\omega_\nu$ is equal to the vector functional $\omega_g$, $g \in \MH$ ([ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_states] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaVectorFunctional]). This functional is normal by [ref:thm:operatorAlgebras_characterizationNormalStates], and, in fact, there is a one-to-one correspondence between $\omega \in \NF{\MFM}$ and $h_\omega \in L^1(X, \mu)_+$ [cite:BR1]. Since $g_\omega \ce \sqrt{h_\omega} \in L^2(X, \mu)$ is well-defined, one may also interpret this as a correspondence $\NF{\MFM} \cong L^2(X, \mu)_+$, where $\omega = \omega_{g_\omega} = \braket{g_\omega, \,\sbullet\ g_\omega}$ is a vector functional.

- For $\MFM = \BO(\MH)$, [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_sigmaWeakTopology] showed that $\cdual{\NO(\MH)} \cong \BO(\MH)$ and $\pdual{\BO(\MH)} \cong \NO(\MH)$ (considering [ref:pro:topologicalVectorSpaces_dualSpaceWeakTopology]), hence $\cdual{(\pdual{\BO(\MH)})} \cong \BO(\MH)$. Thus, in this case the first equivalences of [ref:thm:operatorAlgebras_characterizationNormalStates] are clear. More generally, let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be an arbitrary von Neumann algebra. [ref:thm:operatorAlgebras_characterizationNormalStates] implies that the functionals $\omega_\xi = \braket{\xi, \,\sbullet\ \xi}$, $\xi \in \MH$, and $\omega_\rho = \tr(\rho \ \sbullet\,)$, $\rho \in \DM(\MH)$, from [ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_states] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaVectorFunctional] and [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaNormalState] are normal states on $\MFM$ in the sense of [ref:def:operatorAlgebras_normalState].

### Support of a Normal Functional

[Support projection]#para:operatorAlgebras_support
([cite:StratilaZsido19])
Let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a von Neumann algebra and $\varphi \in \NF{\MFM}$ be a normal functional on $\MFM$. Using spectral theory, one can show the following result [cite:StratilaZsido19].

If $A \in \PE{\MFM}$ is a positive element in $\MFM$ such that $\varphi(A) = 0$, then it follows that $\varphi\bigl(\ssupp(A)\bigr) = 0$, where $\ssupp(A)$ denotes the support of $A$ (introduced in [ref:para:operators_supportPO]). Consequently, the family $\MF \ce \set{P \in \PO(\MFM) \, : \, \varphi(P) = 0}$ is increasingly directed.

Denote the supremum of the family $\MF$ by $P_0 \ce \id_\MH - \ssupp(\varphi) \in \PO(\MFM)$, and let $(P_i)_{i \in I} \subset \MF$ be a net such that $P_i \uparrow P_0$. Using that $\varphi$ is normal ([ref:thm:operatorAlgebras_characterizationNormalStates]), it follows that

$$
\varphi(P_0) = \varphi\sumbra{\bigg}{\sup_{i \in I} P_i} = \sup_{i \in I} \varphi(P_i) = 0 \ .
$$

This shows that $P_0$ is the largest projection in $\MFM$ on which $\varphi$ vanishes. Equivalently, the projection $\ssupp(\varphi) = \id_\MH - P_0$, which is called the ( ) of $\varphi$, is the smallest projection in $\MFM$ satisfying the relation

[equation:eq:operatorAlgebras_supportProjection]
$$
\varphi\bigl(\ssupp(\varphi)\bigr) = \varphi(\id_\MH) \ .
$$

The following two identities are basic consequences of the definition of $\ssupp(\varphi)$ which are often useful. They are stated in [cite:StratilaZsido19] and [cite:Stratila20], respectively.

## Lemma [label:eq:operatorAlgebras_supportInFunctional]

Let $\varphi \in \NF{\MFM}$. For all $A \in \MFM$, there holds

$$
\varphi(A) = \varphi\bigl(A \, \ssupp(\varphi)\bigr) = \varphi\bigl(\ssupp(\varphi) A\bigr) = \varphi\bigl(\ssupp(\varphi) A \, \ssupp(\varphi)\bigr) \ .
$$

## Proof

By linearity of $\varphi$, the definition of $\ssupp(\varphi)$, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality [ref:eq:operatorAlgebras_CS] from [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_formFromState], it follows that

$$
\vabs[\big]{\varphi(A) - \varphi\bigl(A \ssupp(\varphi)\bigr)}^2 = \vabs[\big]{\varphi\bigl(A (\id_\MH - \ssupp(\varphi))\bigr)} \le \varphi(A A^\ast) \, \varphi\bigl(\id_\MH - \ssupp(\varphi)\bigr) = 0
$$

which shows the first equality. The second identity is proved similarly, and third one follows from the first two identities.

## Lemma [label:lem:operatorAlgebras_normalFunctionalZero]

For all $A \in \MFM$, it holds that $\varphi(A^\ast A) = 0 \iff A \, \ssupp(\varphi) = 0$.

## Proof

1. Assume that $\varphi(A^\ast A) = 0$. From [ref:para:operatorAlgebras_support], it follows that $\varphi\bigl(\ssupp(A^\ast A)\bigr) = 0$. Since $\ssupp(A^\ast A) = \rsupp(A)$ [cite:StratilaZsido19], where $\rsupp(A) = \id_\MH - \bigl[\ker(A)\bigr]$ is the right support of $A$ ([ref:para:operators_supportPO]), and $\id_\MH - \ssupp(\varphi)$ is the largest projection in $\MFM$ contained in the kernel of $\varphi$, one obtains

$$
\id_\MH - \bigl[\ker(A)\bigr] \le \id_\MH - \ssupp(\varphi) \ .
$$

This implies $\ssupp(\varphi) \le \bigl[\ker(A)\bigr]$, hence $\ran\bigl(\ssupp(\varphi)\bigr) \subset \ker(A)$ by definition of the order relation for projection operators ([ref:para:operators_orderPO]). It is now an immediate consequence that $A \ssupp(\varphi) = 0$.

2. Conversely, if one assumes that the last identity is satisfied for arbitrary $A \in \MFM$, one computes using [ref:eq:operatorAlgebras_supportInFunctional] that

$$
\varphi(A^\ast A) = \varphi\bigl(A^\ast A \, \ssupp(\varphi)\bigr) = \varphi(0) = 0 \ . \tag*{\qedhere}
$$

One of the most important applications of the support projection is to detect whether a normal functional is faithful. The following is stated in [cite:Stratila20] and [cite:StratilaZsido19].

## Proposition [label:pro:operatorAlgebras_normalFaithful]

The normal functional $\varphi$ is faithful if and only if $\ssupp(\varphi) = \id_\MH$.

## Proof

Assume first that $\varphi$ is faithful, , for all $A \in \MFM$ the implication $\varphi(A^\ast A) = 0 \, \implies \, A = 0$ holds true. By [ref:lem:operatorAlgebras_normalFunctionalZero], this is equivalent to $A \, \ssupp(\varphi) = 0 \, \implies \, A = 0$ for all $A \in \MFM$. In particular, one can choose any projection $P \in \PO(\MFM)$ in place of $A$. But then the identity $P \, \ssupp(\varphi) = 0$ is equivalent to the projections $P$ and $\ssupp(\varphi)$ being orthogonal [cite:Moretti19], hence the previous implication asserts that $\ssupp(\varphi)$ is only orthogonal to the zero projection, that is, $\ran(\ssupp(\varphi))^\perp = \{0\}$. [ref:cor:operators_characterizationPerp] [ref:enu:operators_densePerp] now implies that $\ssupp(\varphi) = \id_\MH$.

Conversely, assume that $\ssupp(\varphi) = \id_\MH$. Relying once again on [ref:lem:operatorAlgebras_normalFunctionalZero], it follows that for all $A \in \MFM$, $\varphi(A^\ast A) = 0 \implies A = 0$, thus $\varphi$ is faithful. This completes the proof.

As another important application, the support of vector functionals, introduced in [ref:exa:operatorAlgebras_states] [ref:enu:operatorAlgebras_exaVectorFunctional], shall be computed; this will yield cyclic projections ([ref:para:operatorAlgebras_cyclicProjections]) [cite:StratilaZsido19].

## Proposition [label:pro:operatorAlgebras_supportVectorFunctional]

Let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a von Neumann algebra, let $\xi \in \MH$ be arbitrary, and let $\omega_\xi = \braket{\xi, \,\sbullet\ \xi}$ be the vector functional induced by $\xi$ on $\MFM$. Denote the same functional on the commutant $\comm{\MFM}$ of the algebra $\MFM$ by $\comm{\omega_\xi} = \braket{\xi, \,\sbullet\ \xi}$. Then

$$
\ssupp(\omega_\xi) = P_\xi = [\comm{\MFM} \xi] \tand \ssupp(\comm{\omega_\xi}) = \comm{P_\xi} = [\MFM \xi] \ .
$$

## Proof

First, it is clear that $\omega_\xi(P_\xi) = \omega_\xi(\id_\MH)$ since $\xi \in [\comm{\MFM} \xi]$, hence $P_\xi$ satisfies the same property as the support $\ssupp(\omega_\xi)$. Therefore, it only remains to show that $P_\xi \le \ssupp(\omega_\xi)$ which, by the minimality of the support projection, then implies $P_\xi = \ssupp(\omega_\xi)$. Recall from [ref:para:operators_orderPO] that the relation $P_\xi \le \ssupp(\omega_\xi)$ is equivalent to $\ran(P_\xi) \subset \ran\bigl(\ssupp(\omega_\xi)\bigr)$. Let $\eta \in \ran(P_\xi)$ be arbitrary, that is, $\eta = \dlim{\MH}{n \to \infty} \comm{A_n} \xi$ for a sequence $(\comm{A_n})_{n \in \N} \subset \comm{\MFM}$. One computes

$$
\ssupp(\omega_\xi) \eta = \dlim{\MH}{n \to \infty} \ssupp(\omega_\xi) \comm{A_n} \xi = \dlim{\MH}{n \to \infty} \comm{A_n} \, \ssupp(\omega_\xi) \xi = \dlim{\MH}{n \to \infty} \comm{A_n} \xi = \eta \ ,
$$

where first continuity of the support, then the fact that $\ssupp(\omega_\xi) \in \PO(\MFM) \subset \MFM$, and finally the identity $\ssupp(\omega_\xi) \xi = \xi$ were used. (Note that the last two properties hold by construction of the support projection.) From [ref:lem:operators_rangeProjection], it now follows that $\eta \in \ran\bigl(\ssupp(\omega_\xi)\bigr)$, and thus the proof of the first identity is complete. For the second relation, one proceeds analogously.

## Corollary [label:cor:operatorAlgebras_faithfulSeparating]

Let $\MFM \subset \BO(\MH)$ be a von Neumann algebra, and let $\varphi = \omega_\xi$ be a vector functional on $\MFM$ induced by $\xi \in \MH$. Then $\varphi$ is faithful if and only if $\xi$ is separating for $\MFM$.

## Proof

By [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_normalFaithful], the normal functional $\varphi$ is faithful if and only if $\ssupp(\varphi) = \id_\MH$, and by [ref:pro:operatorAlgebras_supportVectorFunctional], the support takes the form $\ssupp(\varphi) = [\comm{\MFM} \xi]$. According to [ref:para:operatorAlgebras_cyclicProjections], the condition $[\comm{\MFM} \xi] = \id_\MH$ is equivalent to $\xi$ being separating for $\MFM$.

### The GNS-Construction

#subsec:operatorAlgebras_GNS

## Definition [label:def:operatorAlgebras_representation]

Let $\MFA$ be a $C^\ast$-algebra. A of $\MFA$ is pair $(\MH, \pi)$ consisting of a Hilbert space $\MH$ and a $\ast$-homomorphism $\pi : \MFA \longto \BO(\MH)$. It is called iff $\pi$ is injective. Two $\ast$-representations $(\MH_1, \pi_1)$ and $(\MH_2, \pi_2)$ are said to be iff there exists a unitary operator $U : \MH_1 \longto \MH_2$ such that

$$
\forall A \in \MFA \ : \ \pi_2(A) = U \pi_1(A) U^\ast \ .
$$

A of $\MFA$ is a triple $(\MH, \pi, \Omega)$ consisting of a $\ast$-representation $(\MH, \pi)$ of $\MFA$ and a cyclic vector $\Omega \in \MH$ for the set $\pi(\MFA) \subset \BO(\MH)$, that is, a vector such that $[\pi(\MFA) \Omega] = \MH$.

Let $(\MFA, \idm)$ be a unital $C^\ast$-algebra and $\omega \in \SS(\MFA)$ be an arbitrary state. The goal of this subsection is to construct a specific cyclic representation $(\MH_\omega, \pi_\omega, \Omega_\omega)$ of $\MFA$ such that $\omega = \omega_{\Omega_\omega}$ for a suitable vector $\Omega_\omega \in \MH_\omega$. The following presentation closely follows [cite:BR1].
