# Topological Vector Spaces

{#app:topologicalVectorSpaces}

This first appendix collects some selected notions from general topology and the theory of locally convex spaces, in particular, the concept of weak topologies, which are used in different places throughout the main part of the text.

## Preliminaries from General Topology

\begin{para}[Closure]{#para:topologicalVectorSpaces_topology}
([cite:Voigt20])
Let $X \neq \emptyset$ be a non-empty set and $\MFT \subset \MFP(X)$ be a topology on $X$. Denote the system of closed sets in $(X, \MFT)$ by $\MFC_\MFT \ce \set{C \subset X \ : \ X \setminus C \in \MFT}$. For an arbitrary subset $A \subset X$, one defines the \bemph{closure} of $A$ to be the set

$$
_ (A) \ .
$$

The closure of $A$ is also commonly denoted by $\ol{A}^\MFT$ or $\ol{A}$. It is clear that the closure of $A$ is the smallest closed set containing $A$.
\end{para}

\begin{para}[Comparison of topologies]{#para:topologicalVectorSpaces_comparisonTopologies}
([cite:Waldmann14])
Let $\MFT_1$ and $\MFT_2$ be two topologies on a set $X$. $\MFT_2$ is said to be \bemph{finer} than $\MFT_1$, and $\MFT_1$ is said to be \bemph{coarser} than $\MFT_2$, iff $\MFT_1 \subset \MFT_2$. For every subset $A \subset X$ and every topological space $(Y, \MFS)$, it holds that [cite:Werner18]

$$
_ _2(A) _ _1(A) C^0 ((X, _1), Y ) C^0 ((X, _2), Y ) \ .
$$

Let $\MST(X) \subset \MFP\bigl(\MFP(X)\bigr)$ be the collection of topologies on a set $X$. Define a binary relation $\le$ on $\MST(X)$ by setting $\MFT_1 \le \MFT_2$ iff $\MFT_1 \subset \MFT_2$. It holds that $(\MST(X), \le)$ is a partially ordered set.
\end{para}

## Definition: \protectInitial topology \cite[Def. 3.12 [label:def:topologicalVectorSpaces_initialTopology]

{Querenburg01}}]
Let $X$ be a non-empty set, let $I$ be an index set, and for each $i \in I$ let $(X_i, \MFT_i)$ be a topological space and $f_i : X \longto X_i$ be a map. A topology $\MFT$ on $X$ is called \bemph{initial topology} with respect to $(f_i)_{i \in I}$ iff it satisfies the following universal property:

[label=\normalfont(IT)]

- For an arbitrary topological space $(Y, \MFS)$, a mapping $g : Y \longto X$ is continuous if and only if $f_i \circ g$ is continuous for every $i \in I$.

The initial topology is characterized as follows.

\begin{ntheorem}[\protect{Characterization of the initial topology [cite:Querenburg01]}]{#thm:topologicalVectorSpaces_initialTopology}
Let $X \neq \emptyset$ be a set, let $I$ be an index set, and for each $i \in I$ let $(X_i, \MFT_i)$ be a topological space and $f_i : X \longto X_i$ be a map. There exists a unique initial topology $\MFT$ with respect to $(f_i)_{i \in I}$ on $X$, and it is the coarsest topology for which the family of maps $(f_i)_{i \in I}$ is continuous. In particular, a net $(x_k)_{k \in N}$ converges in $(X, \MFT)$ to $x \in X$ if and only if $f_i(x_k) \to f_i(x)$ in $(X_i, \MFT_i)$ for every $i \in I$.
\end{ntheorem}

## Linear and Weak Topologies

## Definition: Topological vector space [label:def:topologicalVectorSpaces_topVS]

([cite:Voigt20])
Let $E$ be a vector space over a field $\K$ and $\MFT$ be a topology on the underlying set $E$. $\MFT$ is called a \bemph{vector space topology} (or: linear topology), and the pair $(E, \MFT)$ is called a \bemph{topological vector space}, iff the vector space operations $(x, y) \longmto x + y$ and $(\lambda, x) \longmto \lambda x$ are continuous with respect to $\MFT$. The (\bemph{topological}) \bemph{dual space} $\cdual{(E, \MFT)}$ of $E$ (short: $\cdual{E}$) is defined to be the space of all $\MFT$-continuous linear functionals on $E$.

## Proposition: \protect\cite[Thm. 1.5 [label:pro:topologicalVectorSpaces_ITTVS]

{Voigt20}}]
Let $E$ be a vector space, let $\set{(E_i, \MFT_i)}_{i \in I}$ be a family of topological vector spaces, and for every $i \in I$ let $f_i : E \longto E_i$ be a linear map. Then the initial topology $\MFT$ on $E$ with respect to the family $(f_i)_{i \in I}$ is a linear topology.

## Proposition: \protect\cite[p. 7 [label:pro:topologicalVectorSpaces_LCS]

{Voigt20}}]
Let $E$ be a $\K$-vector space and $P$ be a set of semi-norms on $E$. Then the initial topology $\MFT_P$ on $E$ with respect to the mappings $(\id_p)_{p \in P}$, where $\id_p : E \longmto (E, p)$, $x \longmto x$, is a vector space topology on $E$ called the topology generated by $P$. In particular, it holds that a net $(x_i)_{i \in I}$ in $E$ converges to $x \in E$ if and only if

$$
p P \ : \ _i I p(x_i - x) = 0 \ .
$$

\begin{para}[Weak topologies]{#para:topologicalVectorSpaces_weakTopology}
([cite:Voigt20])
A \bemph{dual pair} $\braket{E, F}$ consists of two $\K$-vector spaces $E$ and $F$ and a bilinear mapping $b \equiv \braket{\cdot, \cdot} : E \times F \longto \K$, called the dual pairing. The map $b$ induces the two mappings

$$
b_1 : E (F, ), \ x b_1(x) \ , \\
b_2 : F (E, ), \ y b_2(y) \ .
$$

The \bemph{weak topology} $\sigma(E, F)$ on the space $E$ with respect to the dual pair $\braket{E, F}$ is defined to be the initial topology with respect to the family $(b_2(y))_{y \in F}$; the weak topology $\sigma(F, E)$ on $F$ is defined analogously as the initial topology with respect to $(b_1(x))_{x \in E}$. According to [ref:pro:topologicalVectorSpaces_ITTVS], they both are vector space topologies.
\end{para}

## Proposition: \protect\cite[Thm. 1.8 [label:pro:topologicalVectorSpaces_dualSpaceWeakTopology]

{Voigt20}}]
Let $\braket{E, F}$ be a dual pair. Then $\cdual{\bigl(E, \sigma(E, F)\bigr)} = b_2(F)$.

## Example [label:exa:topologicalVectorSpaces_theWeakTop]

([cite:Conway85])
Let $E$ be a vector space and $\Lambda \subset \Hom(E, \K)$ be a linear subspace of the algebraic dual space of $E$. Define a bilinear mapping $b : E \times \Lambda \longto \K$ by setting $b(x, \varphi) \ce \varphi(x)$. Then the weak topology $\sigma(E, \Lambda)$ on $E$ with respect to $\braket{E, \Lambda}$ is given as the initial topology of $(\varphi)_{\varphi \in \Lambda}$.

Note that for every $\varphi \in \Lambda$, the functional $\abs{\varphi} : E \longto [0, + \infty)$, $x \longmto \abs{\varphi(x)}$, is a semi-norm on $E$. It holds that the topology $\MFT_{P_\Lambda}$ generated by the family $P_\Lambda \ce \{\abs{\varphi} \, : \, \varphi \in \Lambda\}$ and the weak topology $\sigma(E, \Lambda)$ coincide. Furthermore, by [ref:pro:topologicalVectorSpaces_dualSpaceWeakTopology],

$$
= \ .
$$

Let $(E, \MFT)$ be a topological vector space. Then the topology $\sigma(E, \cdual{E})$ is called \bemph{the weak topology} of $E$. It is the coarsest linear topology on $E$ that yields the same dual space as $\MFT$.

\begin{para}[Weak-$\ast$ topology]{#para:topologicalVectorSpaces_weakStar}
([cite:Conway85])
Let $(E, \MFT)$ be a topological vector space, let $x \in E$ be a point and let $\varphi \in \cdual{E}$ be a continuous linear functional. Consider the map $\iota(x) : \cdual{E} \longto \C$ given by $\iota(x)(\varphi) \ce \varphi(x)$. The weak topology on $\cdual{E}$ with respect to $\Lambda \ce \set{\iota(x) \, : \, x \in E} \subset \Hom(\cdual{E}, \K)$ and $\braket{\varphi, \iota(x)} \ce \iota(x)(\varphi)$ is called the \bemph{weak-$\ast$ topology} on $\cdual{E}$ and denoted by $\sigma(\cdual{E}, E)$. Note that according to [ref:exa:topologicalVectorSpaces_theWeakTop], $\sigma(\cdual{E}, E)$ is generated by the family of semi-norms $\set{\abs{\iota(x)} \, : \, x \in E}$ on $\cdual{E}$.
\end{para}

# Hilbert Space Operators

{#app:operators}

In this appendix, several definitions and propositions from (bounded and unbounded) operator theory on Hilbert space shall be collected as they are heavily used in the main part of this text. Throughout, let $\MH \equiv (\MH, \bdot)$ denote a complex Hilbert space, let $\ndot = \bdot^{1/2}$ be the norm on $\MH$, and let $\bigl(\BO(\MH), \ndot_\mop\bigr)$ be the Banach space of bounded linear operators on $\MH$ with the operator norm.

## Bounded Operators

\begin{ntheorem}[\protect{Bounded linear extension [cite:Werner18]}]{#thm:operators_BLT}
Let $D \subset E$ be a dense linear subspace of a normed space $E$, let $F$ be a Banach space, and let $T \in \BO(D, F)$ be a bounded linear operator. Then there exists a unique extension $\wh{T} \in \BO(E, F)$ of $T$, that is, a bounded linear operator such that $\wh{T}|_D = T$, which satisfies $\norm{\wh{T}}_\mop = \norm{T}_\mop$.
\end{ntheorem}

## Definition: \protectTrace-class and Hilbert-Schmidt operators [label:def:operators_NOHS]

([cite:BlanchardBrüning15])
Let $T \in \BO(\MH)$ be a bounded linear operator and $\abs{T} \ce (T^\ast T)^{1/2}$, defined via the functional calculus. $T$ is called a \bemph{trace-class operator} iff there exists an orthonormal basis $(e_i)_{i \in I} \subset \MH$ such that

$$
_tr _i I e_i, e_i = _i I ^1/2 e_i^2 < + \ .
$$

The set of all trace-class operators is denoted by $\NO(\MH)$. Similarly, $T$ is called a \bemph{Hilbert-Schmidt operator}, and the set of all Hilbert-Schmidt operators is denoted by $\HS(\MH)$, iff there exists an orthonormal basis $(e_i)_{i \in I} \subset \MH$ such that

$$
_HS _tr^1/2 = _i I ^2^1/2 = _i I ^1/2 < + \ .
$$

It is evident that $T$ is a Hilbert-Schmidt operator if and only if $T^\ast T$ is a trace-class operator. Furthermore, $\ndot_tr$ and $\ndot_HS$ are independent of the choice of the orthonormal basis [cite:BlanchardBrüning15].

\begin{para}[Trace and Hilbert-Schmidt inner product]{#para:operators_traceHS}
([cite:BlanchardBrüning15])
On the space of trace-class operators, the \bemph{trace} $\tr : \NO(\MH) \longto \K$ is a well-defined bounded linear functional [cite:BlanchardBrüning15] which is given for any orthonormal basis $(e_i)_{i \in I} \subset \MH$ by

$$
(T) _i I T ( ) \ .
$$

Moreover, one can define an inner product on the space of Hilbert-Schmidt operators:

[equation:eq:operators_HSinnerProduct]
$$
_HS (S^ T) = _i I S, T ( ) \ .
$$

\end{para}

## Proposition: \protect\cite[Thm. 26.1 \& 26.2 [label:pro:operators_NOHS]

{BlanchardBrüning15}}]
$\bigl(\NO(\MH), \ndot_tr\bigr)$ and $\bigl(\HS(\MH), \ndot_HS\bigr)$ are normed vector spaces with $\norm{T^\ast}_tr = \norm{T}_tr$ and $\norm{S^\ast}_HS = \norm{S}_HS$ for all $T \in \NO(\MH)$ and $S \in \HS(\MH)$, and they are two-sided $\ast$-ideals in $\BO(\MH)$. Furthermore, $\bigl(\NO(\MH), \ndot_tr\bigr)$ is a Banach space and $\bigl(\HS(\MH), \bdot_HS\bigr)$ is a Hilbert space.

## Definition: Density matrix [label:def:operators_densityMatrix]

([cite:BlanchardBrüning15])
A trace-class operator $\rho \in \NO(\MH)$ is called a \bemph{density matrix} iff $\rho$ is self-adjoint ($\rho^\ast = \rho$), positive ($\braket{\xi, \rho \xi} \ge 0$ for all $\xi \in \MH)$ and normalized ($\norm{\rho}_tr = \tr(\rho) = 1$). The space of all density matrices on $\MH$ is denoted by $\DM(\MH)$.

## Definition: Orthogonal projection [label:def:operators_orthogonalProjections]

An operator $P \in \BO(\MH)$ is called an \bemph{orthogonal projection} (or: projection for short) iff $P^2 = P$ and $\ker(P) \perp \ran(P)$, equivalently, if $P^2 = P$ and $P^\ast = P$ [cite:Werner18]. The set of all orthogonal projections on $\MH$ is denoted by $\PO(\MH)$.

## Lemma: Range of a projection [label:lem:operators_rangeProjection]

Let $P \in \PO(\MH)$. Then $\eta \in \ran(P)$ if and only if $P \eta = \eta$.

## Proof

If $\eta \in \ran(P)$, then there exists $\xi \in \MH$ such that $\eta = P \xi$. Since $P$ is idempotent, it follows that $P \eta = P^2 \xi = P \xi = \eta$. The converse implication is clear.

\begin{ntheorem}[\protect{of the orthogonal projection [cite:Werner18]}]{#thm:operators_orthogonalProjection}
Let $U \subset \MH$ be a closed non-empty subspace. Then there exists a unique non-zero orthogonal projection $P = P_U \in \PO(\MH) \setminus \{0\}$ such that $\ran(P) = U$ and $\ker(P) = U^\perp$. Moreover, the operator $Q \ce \id_\MH - P$ is also an orthogonal projection, and its range is given by $\ran(Q) = \ran(P)^\perp$. Finally, the Hilbert space decomposes into an orthogonal direct sum $\MH = U \oplus U^\perp$.
\end{ntheorem}

## Remark [label:rem:operators_orthogonalProjectionClosedSubspace]

It follows from [ref:thm:operators_orthogonalProjection] that the set $\PO(\MH)$ and the set of closed subspaces of $\MH$ are in one-to-one correspondence by identifying every orthogonal projection $P$ with the closed subspace $U \ce \ran(P) \subset \MH$, and vice versa every closed subspace with the unique orthogonal projection $P_U$ onto it [cite:BlanchardBrüning15]. This justifies using the following notation for any subspace $U \subset \MH$:

$$
[U] P_ _ (U) ( ) \ .
$$

## Corollary [label:cor:operators_characterizationPerp]

Let $U \subset \MH$ be a subspace.

- $\clos_{\ndot}(U) = (U^\perp)^\perp$.

- The following assertion are equivalent:

[equiv]

- $U$ lies dense in $\MH$;

- $U^\perp = \{0\}$;

- $[U] = \id_\MH$.

## Proof

Assertion [ref:enu:operators_closurePerp] is a well-known consequence of the theorem of the orthogonal projection [cite:Werner18]. The first equivalence (i) $\iff$ (ii) in [ref:enu:operators_densePerp] follows from [ref:enu:operators_closurePerp] by noting that $\MH = \{0\}^\perp$, and the equivalence (i) $\iff$ (iii) can be seen by using that $\eta = [U] \eta$ iff $\eta \in \ran([U])$ according to [ref:lem:operators_rangeProjection].

## Lemma [label:lem:operators_projectionRestrictedID]

Let $U \subset \MH$ be a closed subspace and $P \in \PO(\MH)$ be an orthogonal projection such that $P|_U = \id_\MH$. If $U^\perp \subset \ker(P)$, then $P = [U]$.

## Proof

The identity $P|_U = \id_\MH$ implies that $U \subset \ran(P)$ by [ref:lem:operators_rangeProjection]. Since $\ker(P) = \ran(P)^\perp$ ([ref:thm:operators_orthogonalProjection]), it follows from the assumption that $U^\perp \subset \ran(P)^\perp$.

Let $\eta \in \ran(P)$ be arbitrary. Then the previous observation implies that $\eta \perp \xi$ for all $\xi \in U^\perp$, hence $\eta \in (U^\perp)^\perp = \clos_{\ndot}(U) = U$ by [ref:cor:operators_characterizationPerp] [ref:enu:operators_closurePerp] and closedness of $U$. Thus, $\ran(P) = U$ which is equivalent to $P = [U]$.

\begin{para}[Order relation on $\PO(\MH)$]{#para:operators_orderPO}
([cite:Moretti19])
For orthogonal projections $P, Q \in \PO(\MH)$, define the relation $P \le Q$ to hold true if and only if $\ran(P) \subset \ran(Q)$. This gives a partial order on $\MSP(\MH)$ due to the respective properties of the set-theoretic inclusion, \cf{} [ref:rem:operators_orthogonalProjectionClosedSubspace].
\end{para}

\begin{para}[Support projections]{#para:operators_supportPO}
([cite:StratilaZsido19])
Let $T \in \BO(\MH)$. The following projections related to $T$ are of interest:

$$
(T) (T) (T) _ - (T) = \ .
$$

Since $\ker(T) = \ran(T^\ast)^\perp$ [cite:Werner18], it follows that $\rsupp(T) = \lsupp(T^\ast)$, and in case that $T$ is self-adjoint, the \bemph{support} (\bemph{projection}) of $T$ is defined to be

$$
(T) (T) = (T) \ .
$$

\end{para}

## Definition: Partial isometry [label:def:operators_partialIsometry]

([cite:Schmüdgen12], [cite:StratilaZsido19])
Let $\MH_1$ and $\MH_2$ be two Hilbert spaces, and let $\MG_1 \subset \MH_1$ and $\MG_2 \subset \MH_2$ be closed subspaces. A linear operator $V : \MH_1 \longto \MH_2$ that maps the space $\MG_1$ isometrically onto the space $\MG_2$ and annihilates $\MG_1^\perp$ is called a \bemph{partial isometry}. The space $\MG_1$ is called the \bemph{initial space} of $V$, and $\MG_2$ is called the \bemph{final space} of $V$. It holds that $\rsupp(V) = V^\ast V$ is the projection onto $\MG_1$ and $\lsupp(V) = V V^\ast$ is the projection onto $\MG_2$.

## Closed and Closable Operators

## Definition [label:def:operators_closed]

([cite:Schmüdgen12])
Let $T : \MH \supset \dom(T) \longto \MH$ be a linear operator. $T$ is called \bemph{closed} iff its graph $\gr(T) \ce \set{(\xi, T \xi) \, : \, \xi \in \dom(T)}$ is closed in $\MH \oplus \MH$, and it is called \bemph{closable} iff there exists a closed linear operator $S : \MH \supset \dom(S) \longto \MH$ such that $S \supset T$, \ie{}, $\dom(S) \supset \dom(T)$ and $S \xi = T \xi$ for all $\xi \in \dom(T)$. A linear subspace $\MD \subset \dom(T)$ is called a \bemph{core} for the operator $T$ iff for every $\xi \in \dom(T)$, there exists a sequence $(\xi_n)_{n \in \N} \subset \MD$ such that $\xi_n \to \xi$ and $T \xi_n \to T \xi$ in $\MH$.

\begin{para}[Closure of an operator]{#para:operators_closure}
([cite:Schmüdgen12])
Let $T$ be a closable operator and $\overline{T} : \MH \supset \dom(\ol{T}) \longto \MH$ be the closed operator defined by the relation $\gr(\ol{T}) = \ol{\gr(T)}$. This operator, called the \bemph{closure} of $T$, is the smallest closed extension of $T$ with respect to the operator inclusion $\subset$. By construction, $\dom(\ol{T})$ consists of all those $\xi \in \MH$ for which there exists a sequence $(\xi_n)_{n \in \N} \subset \dom(T)$ such that $\xi = \lim_{n \to \infty} \xi_n$ and $\lim_{n \to \infty} T \xi_n$ exists in $\MH$; one defines $\ol{T} \xi \ce \lim_{n \to \infty} T \xi_n$.
\end{para}

\begin{para}[Adjoint operators]
([cite:Schmüdgen12])
Let $T : \MH \supset \dom(T) \longto \MH$ be a densely defined linear operator, \ie{}, $\dom(T) \subset \MH$ lies dense. The \bemph{adjoint operator} $T^\ast : \MH \supset \dom(T^\ast) \longto \MH$ of $T$ is defined by

$$
(T^ ) & \ : \ \ (T) : = \ ,\
$$

T^\ast \xi &\ce \zeta \tfor \xi \in \dom(T^\ast) \ .
$$

[Anti-linear operators]#para:operators_antiLinear
([cite:StratilaZsido19])
An is a mapping $T : \MH \supset \dom(T) \longto \MH$ which satisfies for all $\xi, \eta \in \dom(T)$ and $\alpha, \beta \in \C$

$$
T(\alpha \xi + \beta \eta) = \ol{\alpha} \, T \xi + \ol{\beta} \, T \eta \ .
$$

The of $T$ is the anti-linear operator $T^\ast : \MH \supset \dom(T^\ast) \longto \MH$ defined by

$$
\dom(T^\ast) &\ce \set[\Big]{\xi \in \MH \ : \ \exists \zeta \in \MH \ \forall \eta \in \dom(T) : \braket{x, T \eta} = \braket{\eta, \zeta}} \ ,\
$$
4pt]
T^ & (T^ ) \ .
$$

\end{para}

## Proposition: Properties of $T^\ast$ and $\olT$ \protect\cite[Prop. 1.6 \& Thm. 1.8 [label:pro:operators_propertiesAdjoint]

{Schmüdgen12}}]
Let $T : \MH \supset \dom(T) \longto \MH$ be a densely defined linear operator. The following properties obtain:

- $T^\ast : \MH \supset \dom(T^\ast) \longto \MH$ is a closed linear operator.

- $\ran(T)^\perp = \ker(T^\ast)$.

- $T$ is closable if and only if $T^\ast$ is densely defined.

- If $T$ is closable, then $(\,\ol{T}\,)^\ast = T^\ast$ and $\ol{T} = \dadj{T}$

- Suppose that $\ker(T) = \set{0}$ and that $\ran(T)$ lies dense in $\MH_2$. Then $T^\ast$ is invertible with $(T^\ast)^{-1} = (T^{-1})^\ast$.

- Assume that $T$ is closable and injective. Then $\inv{T}$ is closable if and only if $\ker(\ol{T}) = \{0\}$. In this case, there holds $(\,\ol{T}\,)^{-1} = \ol{(\inv{T})}$.

\begin{ntheorem}[\protect{Polar decomposition of closed operators [cite:Schmüdgen12]}]{#thm:operators_polarDecompositionCO}
Let $T : \MH \supset \dom(T) \longto \MH$ be a densely defined, closed linear operator. Then there exists a partial isometry $U_T : \MH \longto \MH$ with initial space $\ker(T)^\perp = \clos_{\ndot} \ran(T^\ast) = \clos_{\ndot} \ran(\abs{T})$, where $\abs{T} \ce (T^\ast T)^{1/2}$, and final space $\ker(T^\ast)^\perp = \clos_{\ndot} \ran(T)$ such that

$$
T = U_T \ .
$$

This decomposition is unique. Moreover, if $T$ is an anti-linear operator, then the partial isometry $U_T$ is anti-linear as well [cite:StratilaZsido19].
\end{ntheorem}

## Self-adjoint Operators

\begin{ntheorem}[\protect{Spectral thereom for self-adjoint operators [cite:Schmüdgen12]}]
Let $T : \MH \supset \dom(T) \longto \MH$ be a self-adjoint operator. Then there exists a unique spectral measure $E_T : \BO(\R) \longto \PO(\MH)$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\BO(\R)$ such that

$$
T = _ E_T( ) \ .
$$

\end{ntheorem}

## Definition: Spectral integral [label:def:operators_spectralIntegral]

([cite:Schmüdgen12])
Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $\MH$ with spectral measure $E_T$, and let $f : \R \longto \C \cup \set{+ \infty}$ be an $E_T$-almost everywhere finite Borel-measurable function. The \bemph{spectral integral} of $f$ with respect to $E_T$ is denoted by

$$
_T(f) f(T) _ f( ) E_T( ) \ .
$$

For $\xi, \eta \in \MH$, let $\mu_{\xi, \eta}^T : \MB(\R) \longto [0, + \infty]$ be the complex measure $\mu_{\xi, \eta}^T(A) \ce \braket{\xi, E_T(A) \eta}$ on $\MB(\R)$, and set $\mu_\xi^T(A) \ce \mu_{\xi, \xi}^T(A)$. Then the domain of the spectral integral $\I_T(f)$ is given by

$$
( _T(f) ) \ : \ _ ^2 _ ^T( ) < + \ .
$$

## Proposition: \protectProperties of the functional calculus \cite[Thm. 5.9 [label:pro:operators_functionalCalculus]

{Schmüdgen12}}]
Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $\MH$, let $f, g : \R \longto \C \cup \set{+ \infty}$ be two $E_T$-almost everywhere finite Borel-measurable functions, and let $\xi, \eta \in \dom\bigl(\I_T(f)\bigr)$. Then the following properties hold true:

- $\displaystyle \braket{\xi, f(T) \eta} = \int\nolimits_\R f(\lambda) \diff \mu_{\xi, \eta}^T(\lambda)$.

- $\displaystyle \norm{f(T) \xi}^2 = \int\nolimits_\R \abs{f(\lambda)}^2 \diff \mu_\xi^T(\lambda)$.

- $(fg)(T) = \ol{f(T) g(T)}$. If at least one of the functions is bounded, then $(fg)(T) = f(T) g(T)$ [cite:StratilaZsido19], and in this case, the operators $f(T)$ and $g(T)$ commute with each other.

- $\1_A(T) = E_T(A)$ for all $A \in \MB(\R)$.

## Proposition: \protect\cite[Prop. 5.10 [label:pro:operators_eigenvalueSpectralMeasure]

{Schmüdgen12}}]
Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral measure $E_T$. A number $\lambda \in \R$ is an eigenvalue of $T$ if and only if $E_T(\set{\lambda}) \neq 0$, and in this case $E_T(\set{\lambda}) \in \PO(\MH)$ is the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace $\Eig(T, \lambda)$.

## Lemma [label:lem:operators_funcCalcUnitaryConj]

Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $\MH$ and $U \in \UO(\MH)$ be a unitary operator. For a Borel measurable function $\varphi : \sigma(T) \longto \C$, it holds that

$$
(U T U^ ) = U (T) U^ \ .
$$

## Proof

By the multiplication operator form of the spectral theorem [cite:Kaballo14], [cite:RS1], there exists a measure space $(X, \Sigma, \nu)$, a measurable function $g : X \longto \C$, and a unitary operator $V : \MH \longto L^2(X, \nu)$ such that $T = V^\ast M_g V$. Define the unitary $W \ce V U^\ast : \MH \longto L^2(X, \nu)$. One can then write $U T U^\ast = W^\ast M_g W$. From the functional calculus [cite:Kaballo14], it now follows that

$$
(U T U^ ) = (W^ M_g W) = W^ M_ g W = U V^ M_ g V U^ = U (T) U^ \ . *
$$

## Lemma [label:lem:operators_funcCalcEigenvalue]

Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $\MH$ and $\Omega \in \Eig(T, \lambda)$ be an eigenvector of $T$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda \in \R$, \ie{}, $T \Omega = \lambda \Omega$. Then for every $E_T$-almost everywhere finite Borel-measurable function $f : \R \longto \C \cup \set{+ \infty}$, it holds that $f(T) \Omega = f(\lambda) \Omega$.

## Proof

First, note that from [ref:lem:operators_rangeProjection] and [ref:pro:operators_eigenvalueSpectralMeasure], it follows that $E_T(\{\lambda\}) \Omega = \Omega$. Next, recall that if $A \cap B = \emptyset$ for $A, B \in \MB(\R)$, then $E_T(A \cup B) = E_T(A) + E_T(B)$ and $E_T(A) E_T(B) = E_T(B) E_T(A) = 0$ [cite:Schmüdgen12]. Hence, if $\lambda \in A$ for some $A \in \MB(\R)$, then one obtains

$$
E_T(A) = E_T (A ) + E_T( ) = E_T(A ) E_T( ) + = \ .
$$

Similarly, if $\lambda \notin A$, it holds that $E_T(A) \Omega = E_T(A) E_T(\{\lambda\}) \Omega = 0$.

Let $\xi \in \MH$ be arbitrary and consider the complex measure $A \longmto \braket{\xi, E_T(A) \Omega} = \mu_{\xi, \Omega}^T(A)$ on $\MB(\R)$. By the previous two observations, it holds that $\mu_{\xi, \Omega}^T(A) = \braket{\xi, \Omega} \, \delta_\lambda(A)$, where $A \longmto \delta_\lambda(A) = \1_{A}(\lambda)$ is the Dirac measure at $\lambda$. Using [ref:pro:operators_functionalCalculus] [ref:enu:operators_funcCalcIP], one obtains

$$
= _ f(t) = _ f(t) \, _ (t) = \ .
$$

Since $\xi \in \MH$ was arbitrary, this shows that $f(T) \Omega = f(\lambda) \Omega$.

\begin{ntheorem}[\protect{Trotter product formula [cite:RS1], [cite:DJP03]}]{#thm:operators_TrotterProductFormula}
Let $A$ and $B$ be two self-adjoint operators on $\MH$, and assume that the operator sum $A + B$ is essentially self-adjoint on $\dom(A) \cap \dom(B)$. Then the following limit exists in the strong operator topology on $\BO(\MH)$:

[equation:eq:operators_TrotterProductFormula]
$$
^ t (A + B) = n ( ^ t A / n \, ^ t B / n )^n \ .
$$

\end{ntheorem}

## Definition: Strong resolvent convergence [label:def:operators_SRConvergence]

([cite:Oliveira09])
Let $T_n$ ($n \in \N$) and $T$ be self-adjoint operators on $\MH$. One says that the sequence $(T_n)_{n \in \N}$ converges to $T$ in the \bemph{strong resolvent sense} iff $(T_n - \ii)^{-1} \to (T - \ii)^{-1}$ in the strong operator topology, that is,

$$
\ : \ _n (T_n - )^-1 - (T - )^-1 = 0 \ .
$$

## Proposition: \protect\cite[Prop. 10.1.8 \& 10.1.9 [label:pro:operators_characterizationSRConvergence]

{Oliveira09}, [cite:RS1]}]
The following assertions are equivalent:

[equiv]

- $T_n \to T$ in the strong resolvent sense;

- $\ee^{- \ii t T_n} \to \ee^{- \ii t T}$ strongly for all $t \in \R$;

- $f(T_n) \to f(T)$ strongly for all bounded continuous $f : \R \longto \C$.

## Proposition: \protect\cite[Prop. 10.1.13 [label:pro:operators_SOimpliesSR]

{Oliveira09}}]
Let $T_n, T \in \BO(\MH)$ be self-adjoint. If $T_n \to T$ in the strong operator topology, then $T_n \to T$ in the strong resolvent sense.

## Proposition: \protect\cite[Prop. 10.1.18 [label:pro:operators_coreSOimpliesSR]

{Oliveira09}, [cite:RS1], [cite:DJP03]}]
Let $T$ and $(T_n)_{n \in \N}$ be self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space $\MH$. Suppose that $\MD \subset \MH$ is a subspace contained in $\dom(T)$ and $\dom(T_n)$ for all $n \in \N$, and that $T$ is essentially self-adjoint on $\MD$. Furthermore, assume that $\lim_{n \to \infty} T_n \xi = T \xi$ for all $\xi \in \MD$. Then it follows that $T_n \to T$ in the strong resolvent sense.

## Proposition: \protect\cite[Prop. A.4 [label:pro:operators_SRimpliesW]

{DJP03}}]
Let $(T_n)_{n \in \N}$ be a sequence of self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space $\MH$, and assume that there exists another self-adjoint operator $T$ such that $T_n \to T$ in the strong resolvent sense. Furthermore, suppose that $(\Omega_n)_{n \in \N} \subset \MH$ and $\Omega \in \MH$ are vectors such that $\Omega_n \to \Omega$ weakly, and that there exists a constant $C \ge 0$ such that for all $n \in \N$, $\norm{T_n \Omega_n} \le C$. Then $\Omega \in \dom(T)$, $\dlim{w}{n \to \infty} T_n \Omega_n$ exists, and $T \Omega = \dlim{w}{n \to \infty} T_n \Omega_n$.

## Remark [label:rem:operators_SRimpliesW]

([cite:DJP03])
Suppose that $\dlim{w}{n \to \infty} T_n \Omega_n$ exists. Then it follows from the uniform boundedness principle that $(T_n \Omega_n)_{n \in \N} \subset \MH$ is bounded [cite:Werner18], \ie{}, there is a constant $C \ge 0$ such that $\norm{T_n \Omega_n} \le C$ for all $n \in \N$. Therefore, one may replace the assumption $\norm{T_n \Omega_n} \le C$ in the above proposition by the existence of $\dlim{w}{n \to \infty} T_n \Omega_n$.

## Lemma [label:lem:operators_SRimpliesFSR]

Let $(T_n)_{n \in \N}$ be a sequence of self-adjoint operators on $\MH$ converging in the strong resolvent sense to a self-adjoint operator $T$. Then for any continuous real-valued function $g : \R \longto \R$, it holds that $g(T_n) \to g(T)$ as $n \to + \infty$ in the strong resolvent sense.\footnote{The author wishes to thank Professor Dr.~Jan Derezi\'{n}ski for clarifying this result and for discussing its proof.}

## Proof

Let $z \in \C \setminus \R$ be arbitrary, and observe that the function $h_z : \R \longto \C$, $\lambda \longmto \bigl(g(\lambda) - z\bigr)^{-1}$, is continuous and bounded. Indeed, since clearly $\abs{g(\lambda) - z} \ge \abs{\Im(z)}$, one obtains

$$
\ .
$$

Therefore, since $T_n \to T$ in the strong resolvent sense, it follows from [ref:pro:operators_characterizationSRConvergence] that $h_z(T_n) \to h_z(T)$ as $n \to + \infty$ in the strong operator topology. But $h_\ii(T_n) = (g(T_n) - \ii)^{-1}$ and $h_\ii(T) = (g(T) - \ii)^{-1}$, hence the previous statement is equivalent to convergence $g(T_n) \to g(T)$ in the strong resolvent sense.

# Quadratic Forms and Self-adjoint Operators

{#app:forms}

In this final appendix, some definitions and results from the theory of positive quadratic forms will be outlined. Again, $\MH \equiv (\MH, \braket{\cdot, \cdot})$ shall denote a complex Hilbert space, and $\ndot = \bdot^{1/2}$ the norm induced by the inner product.

## Closed and Closable Quadratic Forms

## Definition: Quadratic form [label:def:forms_quadraticForm]

([cite:Hiai21])
A \bemph{positive quadratic form} on $\MH$ is a mapping $\MFq : \MH \supset \dom(\MFq) \longto [0, + \infty)$ which satisfies for all $\xi, \eta \in \dom(\MFq)$ and $\lambda \in \C$ the following identities:

$$
( ) = ^2 ( ) ( + ) + ( - ) = 2 ( ) + 2 ( ) \ .
$$

The subspace $\dom(\MFq) \subset \MH$ is called the \bemph{domain} of $\MFq$; if it lies dense in $\MH$, then the quadratic form $\MFq$ is said to be \bemph{densely defined}.

## Definition: Closed and closable form [label:def:forms_closedClosableForm]

([cite:Hiai21], [cite:Schmüdgen12])
A positive quadratic form $\MFq$ on $\MH$ is called \bemph{closed} iff $(\xi_n)_{n \in \N} \subset \dom(\MFq)$, $\xi \in \dom(\MFq)$, $\lim_{n \to \infty} \xi_n = \xi$ and $\lim_{n, k \to \infty} \MFq(\xi_n - \xi_k) = 0$ implies that $\xi \in \dom(\MFq)$ and $\lim_{n \to \infty} \MFq(\xi_n - \xi) = 0$. The form $\MFq$ is said to be \bemph{closable} iff there exists a closed positive quadratic form $\MFt$ on $\MH$ which is an extension of $\MFq$, that is, $\dom(\MFq) \subset \dom(\MFt)$ and $\MFt(\xi) = \MFq(\xi)$ for all $\xi \in \dom(\MFq)$.

## Definition: Lower semi-continuity [label:def:forms_semiContinuity]

([cite:Schmüdgen12])
Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space. An extended real-valued function $f : X \longto \R \cup \{+ \infty\}$ is called \bemph{lower semi-continuous} iff for every sequence $(x_n)_{n \in \N}$ in $X$ which converges to some element $x \in X$, there holds

$$
f(x) _n f(x_n) \ .
$$

## Proposition: \protectCharacterization of closable forms \cite[Thm. A.12 [label:pro:forms_closableForms]

{Hiai21}, [cite:Schmüdgen12]}]
Let $\MFq$ be a positive quadratic form on $\MH$. The following assertions are equivalent:

[equiv]

- $\MFq$ is closable.

- $\MFq$ is lower semi-continuous on $\dom(\MFq)$.

- For every sequence $(\xi_n)_{n \in \N} \subset \dom(\MFq)$ satisfying $\dlim{\MH}{n \to \infty} \xi_n = 0$ and $\lim_{n, m \to \infty} \MFq(\xi_n - \xi_m) = 0$, there holds $\lim_{n \to \infty} \MFq(\xi_n) = 0$.

\begin{para}[Closure of a form]{#para:forms_closure}
([cite:Hiai21], [cite:Schmüdgen12])
Let $\MFq$ be a closable positive quadratic form. Define $\dom(\ol{\MFq}) \ce \set[\big]{\xi \in \MH \, : \, \exists (\xi_n)_{n \in \N} \subset \dom(\MFq) \ \text{s.t.} \ \norm{\xi_n - \xi} \to 0 \ \text{and} \ \MFq(\xi_n - \xi_m) \to 0} \subset \MH$ and the mapping $\ol{\MFq} : \MH \supset \dom(\ol{\MFq}) \longto [0, + \infty)$ by $\ol{\MFq}(\xi) \ce \lim_{n \to \infty} \MFq(\xi_n)$ for $\xi \in \dom(\ol{\MFq})$. This is a well-defined positive quadratic form. Furthermore, one can show that $\ol{\MFq}$ is closed, and that it is the smallest closed extension of the form $\MFq$. Therefore, one calls $\ol{\MFq}$ the \bemph{closure} of $\MFq$.
\end{para}

## The Form Representation Theorem

\begin{para}[Order relation for self-adjoint operators]{#para:forms_orderRelation}
([cite:Hiai21], [cite:Schmüdgen12])
Let $T$ and $S$ be two positive self-adjoint linear operators on $\MH$. Define the relation $S \le T$ to be satisfied iff

[equation:eq:forms_orderRelation]
$$
(T^1/2 ) (S^1/2 ) S^1/2 T^1/2 \ .
$$

\end{para}

\begin{ntheorem}[\protect{Form representation theorem [cite:Hiai21], [cite:Schmüdgen12]}]{#thm:forms_formReprThm}
Let $\MFq : \MH \supset \dom(\MFq) \longto [0, + \infty)$ be a densely defined positive quadratic form. Then $\MFq$ is closed if and only if there exists a positive self-adjoint operator $Q_\MFq : \MH \supset \dom(Q_\MFq) \longto \MH$ such that

[equation:eq:forms_formReprThm]
$$
(Q_ ^1/2 ) = ( ) (Q_ ^1/2 ) \, : \, ( ) = Q_ ^1/2 ^2 \ .
$$

\end{ntheorem}

\begin{para}[Operator associated with a positive form]{#para:forms_fromFormToOp}
([cite:Hiai21])
Let $\MFq : \MH \supset \dom(\MFq) \longto [0, + \infty)$ be a densely defined positive quadratic form. If $\MFq$ is lower semi-continuous, then [ref:pro:forms_closableForms] implies that the closure $\ol{\MFq}$ (\cf{} [ref:para:forms_closure]) is well-defined. Applying [ref:thm:forms_formReprThm] to this closed form, one obtains a positive self-adjoint operator $T \ce Q_{\ol{\MFq}} : \MH \supset \dom(T) \longto \MH$ satisfying [ref:eq:forms_formReprThm]. Since the closure $\ol{\MFq}$ is, in particular, an extension of $\MFq$, it follows that

[equation:eq:forms_fromFormToOp]
$$
(T^1/2 ) ( ) ( ) = T^1/2 ( ) \ .
$$

Moreover, it holds that $T$ is the largest positive self-adjoint linear operator, with respect to the order relation [ref:eq:forms_orderRelation], which satisfies the properties [ref:eq:forms_fromFormToOp], and, furthermore, $\dom(\MFq)$ is a core for the self-adjoint operator $T^{1/2}$ ([ref:def:operators_closed]). To see this, assume that $S$ were another positive self-adjoint operator on $\MH$ satisfying the relations [ref:eq:forms_fromFormToOp]. For every $\xi \in \dom(T^{1/2}) = \dom(\ol{\MFq})$, there exists a sequence $(\xi_n)_{n \in \N} \subset \dom(\MFq)$ such that $\norm{\xi_n - \xi} \to 0$ and $\MFq(\xi_n) \to \ol{\MFq}(\xi)$ as $n \to + \infty$ ([ref:para:forms_closure]). Therefore, from the lower semi-continuity of $\MFq$, it follows that

$$

$$

hence $S \le T$ according to [ref:para:forms_orderRelation]. For the second statement, note that by definition of the closure $\ol{\MFq}$ ([ref:para:forms_closure]) also $\MFq(\xi_n - \xi_m) \to 0$ as $n, m \to + \infty$. Therefore,

$$

$$
